countries.name: Hungary
countries.tagline: Volcanic hills, river mists and a thousand years of stubbornness: the home of Tokaji, the wine that taught Europe to drink noble rot.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026): 58 kha of vineyard (prelim.), 3.0 mhl produced in 2025, 14th in the OIV production table. Eurostat counts 56.8 kha of vines for 2025.

countries.overview:
Hungary fills the western half of the Carpathian Basin, a great bowl rimmed by mountains that keep out the worst of the northern cold and trap the continental summer heat. Inside it, three things decide where good wine grows: water, volcanoes and loess. The Danube, the Tisza, the Bodrog and Lake Balaton temper frosts and, in autumn, breathe out the mists that make noble rot possible. A chain of extinct volcanoes, from the basalt buttes around Balaton to Somló, the rhyolite tuff of Eger, the andesite of the Mátra and the Zemplén Hills of Tokaj, gives the country its most mineral, long-lived whites. Wind-blown loess dresses the slopes of Szekszárd, Tokaj hill and much of the south, and pure sand covers the Great Plain, where vines survived the phylloxera that killed everything else.

The numbers are modest but solid. The OIV counted about 58,000 ha of vineyard in 2025 and 3.0 million hl of wine, which put Hungary 14th among the world's producers. The law divides the vineyard into 22 wine districts (borvidék) grouped into six regions: Tokaj on its own, the Balaton region, Upper Hungary (Eger, Mátra, Bükk), Northern Pannonia (Sopron to Etyek-Buda), the Pannon region of the south (Villány, Szekszárd, Pécs, Tolna) and the Danube region of the Great Plain (Kunság, Csongrád, Hajós-Baja). Each district is a protected designation of origin, and a dozen narrower or broader PDOs sit inside or across them, from tiny Tihany to the umbrella names Balaton, Duna and Pannon.

What makes Hungary thrilling for a wine nerd is its cast of grapes. Furmint, late-ripening, high in acid and hungry for botrytis, is the backbone of Tokaj and increasingly a serious dry white elsewhere. Hárslevelű adds lime-blossom perfume. Olaszrizling (Welschriesling) is the everyday white of Balaton and Somló. Kékfrankos (Blaufränkisch) is the red workhorse from Sopron to Eger, and Kadarka, a fragile, peppery red brought north by Serbs fleeing the Ottomans, is coming back in Szekszárd and Eger. Then come the rarities: Juhfark on Somló, Kéknyelű on Badacsony, Ezerjó at Mór, Sárfehér on the sands of Izsák, plus a raft of 20th-century crossings such as Irsai Olivér and Cserszegi fűszeres.

Tokaj is the reason the world knows Hungarian wine. Its sweet Aszú, made by steeping hand-picked botrytised berries in wine or fermenting must, was famous at the courts of France, Austria, Poland and Russia by the early 18th century. The region was classified vineyard by vineyard between roughly 1700 and 1772 and fenced off as a closed production zone by royal decree in 1737, which makes it one of the first legally protected wine regions anywhere. Eger has its Bull's Blood and a siege legend, Villány has become Central Europe's Cabernet Franc capital, and Szekszárd's loess makes the silkiest reds in the country.

History has not been kind, and that is part of the story in every glass. Phylloxera arrived in the 1880s and pushed planting onto the louse-proof sands of the Great Plain. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon handed slices of historic vineyard to Czechoslovakia, Romania and Yugoslavia. Four decades of Communism merged thousands of growers into state farms and cooperatives that made oxidised, pasteurised volume for the Soviet bloc. Since 1990 foreign capital (much of it French, Spanish and British, starting in Tokaj) and a new generation of family wineries have rebuilt quality, mapped single vineyards (dűlők) and revived old varieties.

Reading a Hungarian label is simple once you know three words. *Bor* is wine, *dűlő* is a named single vineyard, and the district name usually appears with the adjectival suffix -i (Tokaji, Egri, Villányi). Sweetness words matter: *száraz* (dry), *félszáraz* (off-dry), *félédes* (medium) and *édes* (sweet). Above all, look for Tokaji Aszú and dry Furmint from a named dűlő: they are the country's two great contributions to the modern cellar.

history.title: Vines of Roman Pannonia
history.text: Roman soldiers and settlers planted vineyards across Pannonia, the province west of the Danube; by the 5th century records describe extensive vineyards. The Roman towns of Sopianae (Pécs) and Savaria laid down the map that the Sopron, Pécs and Balaton districts still follow.

history.title: Benedictines take up the vine
history.text: The Benedictine archabbey of Pannonhalma (996) and the abbey of Tihany on Lake Balaton (1055) became the first great institutional vineyard owners of the young Christian kingdom. Pannonhalma still makes wine on the hill below the abbey.

history.title: Tatars, then Latin settlers in Tokaj
history.text: The Mongol (Tatar) invasion of 1241 wrecked the vineyards of the Tokaj hills. Béla IV invited 'Latin' settlers, Walloon and Italian, whose memory survives in village names such as Olaszliszka and Bodrogolaszi ('olasz' means Italian).

history.title: The siege of Eger and Bull's Blood
history.text: István Dobó's small garrison held Eger castle against a vast Ottoman army. A later legend says the defenders drank red wine before battle and the Turks, seeing their stained beards, believed the Hungarians drank bull's blood. The name Bikavér appears only centuries later, but the story sells wine to this day.

history.title: First written mention of aszú
history.text: In 2002 the historian István Zelenák found aszú grape wine in the 1571 inheritance letter of Máté Garai. Balázs Szikszai Fabricius's dictionary of 1576 also records it. Aszú was therefore a known product two generations before the famous legend.

history.title: The Oremus legend
history.text: Tradition credits the Reformed pastor Máté Szepsi Laczkó with making an aszú from grapes of the Oremus vineyard at Sátoraljaújhely for Princess Zsuzsanna Lorántffy at Easter. Historians now treat it as legend: Szepsi's own chronicle never mentions aszú. The story still names Tokaj's most mythic vineyard.

history.title: Vineyards ranked by class
history.text: Surveys of the Rákóczi era were followed by János Matolai and Mátyás Bél's three-class ranking in the 1720s and 1730s, completed by the censuses of 1765 and 1772. Sites such as Oremus were rated primae classis. Antal Szirmay refined the ranking again in 1798.

history.title: Wine of kings, king of wines
history.text: Prince Ferenc II Rákóczi, leading Hungary's war of independence against the Habsburgs, used Tokaji as diplomatic currency and sent it to Louis XIV. The phrase 'Vinum Regum, Rex Vinorum' is traditionally attributed to the French king.

history.title: A closed wine region
history.text: On 1 October 1737 King Charles VI (Károly III of Hungary) defined which towns could call their wine Tokaji and required permission to plant. The Tokaj product specification calls it the first definition of a protected origin in the world.

history.title: The Russian commission
history.text: A Russian wine-buying commission sat in Tokaj for most of the 18th century to keep the imperial court in St Petersburg supplied, leasing vineyards and buying the best Aszú and Eszencia.

history.title: Phylloxera and the sands
history.text: Phylloxera spread from 1882 and reached Tokaj by 1885. Because the louse cannot survive in loose sand, the state planted a demonstration vineyard at Miklóstelep near Kecskemét in 1883, and the Great Plain sands became the country's biggest vineyard. In the same years József Törley moved his sparkling wine business from Reims to Budafok (1882).

history.title: Trianon cuts the map
history.text: The Treaty of Trianon gave about two-thirds of the kingdom's territory to neighbours, including a strip of the Tokaj hills now in Slovakia and historic vineyards in Transylvania, Vojvodina and Burgenland.

history.title: State farms and the Borkombinát
history.text: Communist collectivisation merged growers into state farms and cooperatives. In Tokaj a single state combine controlled bottling and sales while up to 6,000 smallholders sold it grapes. Overcropping, pasteurisation and oxidative styles for Soviet-bloc markets damaged the region's name for decades.

history.title: The Tokaj renaissance
history.text: Royal Tokaji (1990) was the first Western joint venture, followed by AXA Millésimes at Disznókő (1992), Vega Sicilia at Oremus (1993) and French investors at Hétszőlő, Pajzos and Megyer. Their capital, and István Szepsy's example, restarted modern Tokaj.

history.title: EU entry and new Tokaj rules
history.text: Hungary joined the EU in 2004 and won exclusive use of the Tokaj name from Italy's Tocai and Alsace's Tokay. In 2013 Tokaj raised the Aszú minimum to 120 g/l of residual sugar, which ended the old 3 and 4 puttonyos levels in practice.

countries.classification:
Hungary uses the EU system with its own vocabulary. A PDO is an *oltalom alatt álló eredetmegjelölés* (OEM) and a PGI is an *oltalom alatt álló földrajzi jelzés* (OFJ). Each of the 22 wine districts is an OEM, and so are a few smaller or broader names: single-village PDOs such as Tihany, Káli, Csopak and Monor, variety-and-place names such as Debrői Hárslevelű and Izsáki Arany Sárfehér, and regional umbrellas such as Balaton, Duna and Pannon. Recent additions include Kőszeg (2025), Etyeki pezsgő for Etyek sparkling wine (2025) and Füred (2025).

The rules are written in a product specification (*termékleírás*) for each PDO and enforced by the local growers' councils (*hegyközség*), which keep the vineyard cadastre. Only land rated Class I or II in that cadastre may produce PDO wine. Many districts now use quality pyramids: Eger's Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior for Bikavér and Csillag; Villány's Classicus, Prémium and the Villányi Franc category; and Somló, Szekszárd and Csopak with similar tiers. Villány pioneered the Latin label term DHC (*Districtus Hungaricus Controllatus*).

Named single vineyards (*dűlő*) may appear on labels only if listed in the PDO's annex; in Tokaj the dűlő wine must be 100% from that site and vintage and the yield is capped at 6 t/ha. Tokaj also has its own legally defined styles (*borkülönlegességek*): Eszencia, Aszú, Szamorodni, Fordítás and Máslás.
countries.climate_soils:
The Carpathian arc shelters the basin from the north and east, so the climate is continental with hot summers, cold winters and a long, often dry autumn. Annual rainfall runs from about 500 mm on the Great Plain to 700 mm in the west. Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe, moderates its shores and reflects light onto the slopes above. The rivers matter most in Tokaj, where the Bodrog and Tisza meet below Tokaj hill and send up morning fogs that alternate with warm afternoons: the perfect cycle for *Botrytis cinerea*.

Soils follow geology. Miocene volcanism left rhyolite, andesite and dacite tuffs, basalt buttes and in places zeolite, perlite and quartzite; weathered, these give the heavy red-brown clays Hungarians call *nyirok*. Loess, fine wind-blown silt, covers Szekszárd, parts of Villány and the southern face of Tokaj hill and gives softer, earlier-ripening wines. Limestone and dolomite run through Villány, Etyek, Mór and the Balaton Uplands, red Permian sandstone colours the soil at Balatonfüred-Csopak, and the Great Plain is pure Danube sand.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.note: Hungary's signature white: late-ripening, high-acid, thick-flavoured and very susceptible to noble rot. The backbone of Tokaji Aszú and of the new wave of dry single-vineyard wines; also grown on Somló and around Balaton.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.note: 'Linden leaf': Tokaj's second grape, adding honeyed, floral perfume to Aszú; has its own PDO at Debrő in the Mátra foothills and makes fine dry wines on Somló and in Villány.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.note: Welschriesling, unrelated to Riesling. The everyday and sometimes great white of Balaton, Csopak and Somló, with bitter almond on the finish.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.note: Blaufränkisch, the most important red grape: crunchy, spicy wines in Sopron, the core of Egri Bikavér, and a growing force in Szekszárd and Mátra.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.note: Thin-skinned, late, peppery Balkan red (Gamza in Bulgaria) brought north in Ottoman times; once the soul of Szekszárd and Eger Bull's Blood, now revived from old clonal selections.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: Villány's star since the 2010s, with its own Villányi Franc category; also strong in Szekszárd and Eger.

grapes.name: Juhfark
grapes.note: 'Sheep's tail', named for its long cylindrical bunches; the austere, smoky white of Somló.

grapes.name: Kéknyelű
grapes.note: 'Blue stalk', a rare Badacsony white with functionally female flowers that needs a pollinator such as Budai zöld planted beside it.

grapes.name: Sárgamuskotály
grapes.note: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, the aromatic third grape of Tokaj.

grapes.name: Kövérszőlő
grapes.note: 'Fat grape', a rare Tokaj variety identical to Romania's Grasă de Cotnari.

grapes.name: Zéta and Kabar
grapes.note: Tarcal-bred crossings for botrytis: Zéta (Furmint x Bouvier, formerly sold as Oremus) and Kabar (Hárslevelű x Bouvier).

grapes.name: Ezerjó
grapes.note: 'Thousand goods', the sharp, crisp white of Mór.

grapes.name: Sárfehér
grapes.note: High-acid white of the Great Plain sands, protected as Izsáki Arany Sárfehér.

grapes.name: Cserszegi fűszeres and Irsai Olivér
grapes.note: Aromatic 20th-century crossings for fresh, early-drinking whites; Cserszegi fűszeres was bred at Keszthely.

countries.name: Slovenia
countries.tagline: A small country with three wine worlds: Collio's mirror in Brda, the bora-swept Karst, and the steep Styrian hills where the world's oldest vine still fruits.

stats.note: Vineyard area: Eurostat apro_cpsh1, 13.9 kha in 2025 (the ministry cites about 17,000 ha cultivated and 14,600 ha registered). Production: OIV figure of 512,800 hl for 2024.

countries.overview:
Slovenia packs Alpine, Mediterranean, Pannonian and Dinaric landscapes into a country smaller than New Jersey, and its wine follows those seams. There are three regions. Primorska in the west runs from the Italian border at Goriška Brda through the Vipava valley and the limestone Karst to the Istrian coast at Koper; it is a continuation of Friuli's Collio and Carso, with Rebula (Ribolla Gialla), Malvazija, Refošk and the local Zelen and Pinela. Podravje in the north-east, the Drava basin, is Styrian and Pannonian country of steep, terraced hills (Štajerska Slovenija, plus Prekmurje beyond the Mura) making crisp, aromatic whites: Laški rizling, Šipon (Furmint), Sauvignon Blanc, Renski rizling, Traminec and Ranina. Posavje in the south-east, along the Sava and Krka, is the land of light, tart blends: Cviček, Metliška črnina, Bizeljčan.

Vineyards cover roughly 14,000 to 17,000 ha depending on who is counting, worked by more than 27,000 holdings averaging just over half a hectare. Production runs around 0.5 million hl; about three-quarters is white, most is drunk at home, and up to 70% carries a geographical designation. The structure is very small-scale: thousands of weekend vineyards (*zidanice*, small vineyard cottages, dot the hills) next to a few large cooperatives such as Klet Brda, Vinakoper, Ptujska klet and Radgonske gorice.

Why does a country this small matter to a wine nerd? Partly because it sits on so many borders. Brda is the same hill system as Italy's Collio, cut by a frontier drawn in 1947 that left families with vines on both sides; the Karst runs straight into Italy's Carso; Štajerska is the southern half of historical Styria, whose northern half is Austria's Südsteiermark; Prekmurje looks across to Hungary. Comparing wines across those lines is one of the best lessons in terroir versus culture that Europe offers.

Slovenia's outsized fame comes from the west. Along the Italian border, growers such as Movia, Klinec, Batič, Kabaj, Čotar and Mlečnik, alongside their friends across the border in Oslavia, revived long skin-contact fermentation of white grapes in the 1990s and 2000s, and the Brda-Collio-Vipava axis became the heartland of modern 'orange wine'. In the east, the Styrian hills around Jeruzalem, Ormož and Haloze make some of Europe's most precise, high-acid whites and fine sweet wines (*ledeno vino*, ice wine, and *suhi jagodni izbor*, the Trockenbeerenauslese equivalent). Maribor has the world's oldest productive vine, more than 400 years old, and Ptuj has the country's oldest cellar and oldest bottled wine.

history.title: Celts and Illyrians
history.text: The ministry and most histories date local winemaking to Celtic and Illyrian tribes, well before the Romans.

history.title: Roman Poetovio
history.text: Roman Poetovio (Ptuj) on the Drava and the colonies of Istria and the Vipava valley spread viticulture; Ptuj was a major legionary town and trading hub.

history.title: The Minorite cellar of Ptuj
history.text: Ptujska klet traces its symbolic beginning to 1239, when the Minorite friars built a monastery in the centre of Ptuj with a wine cellar beneath it.

history.title: The Old Vine of Maribor
history.text: A Žametovka vine planted on the south wall of a house in Maribor's Lent quarter survived Ottoman raids, phylloxera and war; it is now more than 400 years old and listed by Guinness as the oldest vine in the world.

history.title: Slovenian sparkling wine
history.text: Clotar Bouvier began traditional-method sparkling wine at Gornja Radgona in 1852, the start of what became Radgonske gorice's Zlata Radgonska penina. The Bouvier grape (Ranina) carries his name.

history.title: Phylloxera
history.text: Phylloxera ravaged the Habsburg-ruled Slovenian lands; replanting on American rootstocks favoured international varieties, with local grapes such as Žametovka and Rebula surviving in blends.

history.title: Independence and the EU
history.text: Slovenia was the first Yugoslav republic to leave the federation (1991) and joined the EU in 2004. Cooperatives were restructured and family estates grew quickly.

history.title: The orange wine revival
history.text: Growers on both sides of the Brda-Collio border, from Movia and Batič to Gravner and Radikon in Italy, returned to long skin maceration of white grapes, making Slovenia a reference point for 'orange' or macerated white wine.

countries.classification: Slovenia's quality categories (ZGP, *vino z zaščitenim geografskim poreklom*: PDO wine) are tied to its nine wine districts, each a PDO: Goriška Brda, Vipavska dolina, Kras and Slovenska Istra in Primorska; Štajerska Slovenija and Prekmurje in Podravje; Bizeljsko Sremič, Dolenjska and Bela krajina in Posavje. Within PDO wine a label may say *kakovostno vino ZGP* (quality wine) or *vrhunsko vino ZGP* (premium wine, tasting-scored and stricter), and the Prädikat-style terms *pozna trgatev* (late harvest), *izbor*, *jagodni izbor*, *suhi jagodni izbor* and *ledeno vino* apply to sweet wines. Five wines have special status as PTP (*priznano tradicionalno poimenovanje*, recognised traditional designation), each also an EU PDO: Teran (Refošk from the Karst), Cviček (Dolenjska), Metliška črnina and Belokranjec (Bela krajina) and Bizeljčan (Bizeljsko Sremič). A new Wine Act was adopted as a government bill in November 2025 and was in parliament during 2026.
countries.climate_soils: Primorska is sub-Mediterranean: warm summers, mild winters and the cold bora wind that sweeps down the Vipava valley. Its soils are flysch (*opoka*, layered marl and sandstone) in Brda and Vipava and red *terra rossa* over limestone on the Karst. Podravje and Posavje are continental and cooler, with steep marl, sandstone and clay hills; Haloze and Jeruzalem have some of the steepest terraces in Central Europe, and Bizeljsko has quartz sands soft enough to dig storage caves (*repnice*).

grapes.name: Rebula
grapes.note: Ribolla Gialla: the signature white of Goriška Brda, both fresh and long-macerated.

grapes.name: Laški rizling
grapes.note: Welschriesling, the most planted grape, from fresh Styrian whites to botrytised sweet wines.

grapes.name: Šipon
grapes.note: The Styrian name for Furmint, high-acid and long-lived around Jeruzalem and Ormož.

grapes.name: Refošk
grapes.note: Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso: becomes Teran on the Karst's terra rossa and makes a fruity red in Istria.

grapes.name: Malvazija
grapes.note: Istrian Malvasia, the coastal white of Slovenska Istra and Brda.

grapes.name: Zelen and Pinela
grapes.note: Vipava natives: Zelen is herbal and green-fruited, Pinela delicate and nervy.

grapes.name: Vitovska
grapes.note: Karst white grown on terra rossa, often macerated.

grapes.name: Žametovka
grapes.note: Old red variety, the grape of Maribor's Old Vine and a base of Cviček.

grapes.name: Modra frankinja
grapes.note: Blaufränkisch, the main red of Posavje.

grapes.name: Ranina
grapes.note: Bouvier, named for Radgona and Clotar Bouvier.

countries.name: Croatia
countries.tagline: Zinfandel's homeland, cliff-hung Plavac Mali, island whites with Greek roots, and the Graševina plains of Slavonia.

stats.note: Vineyard area: Eurostat apro_cpsh1, 19.1 kha in 2025. Production: 458,000 hl in 2024 (OIV figure as reported by Wine Plus).

countries.overview:
Croatia is two wine countries joined at the hip. Along the Adriatic, Istria and Dalmatia are Mediterranean: limestone, sun, sea light and a thousand islands, with native grapes that taste of herbs and salt. Inland, the Pannonian plain and the hills around Zagreb are Central European: cool nights, loess and marl, and crisp whites led by Graševina (Welschriesling). Wines of Croatia divides the country into four regions: Istria and Kvarner, Dalmatia, the Croatian Uplands and Slavonia with the Croatian Danube. Under EU law there are 18 wine PDOs: three broad regional names (Eastern Continental, Western Continental and Coastal Croatia), twelve subregions such as Hrvatska Istra, Slavonija and Srednja i Južna Dalmacija, and three small site appellations: Dingač, Ponikve and Muškat momjanski.

The vineyard area is about 19,000 ha and falling slowly, and production is around 0.4 to 0.5 million hl. Most farms are tiny, and Croatians drink the bulk of their wine at home, which helps explain why Croatian wine prices are high for the region. The industry has been rebuilt since the 1991 to 1995 war, which hit the Danube vineyards around Vukovar and Ilok especially hard, and since EU entry in 2013 a generation of small estates has emerged on the coast and in Slavonia.

The coastal grapes are the treasure. Plavac Mali, the great red of Dalmatia, grows on vertiginous south-facing slopes such as Dingač and Postup on the Pelješac peninsula, where it ripens to 15% alcohol or more. In 2001 a DNA team led by Carole Meredith, working with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the University of Zagreb, found that a nearly vanished Dalmatian vine, Crljenak Kaštelanski, was identical to California's Zinfandel and Italy's Primitivo, and that it was a parent of Plavac Mali. The old name Tribidrag appears in a Dalmatian record of 1444. White grapes are just as local: Pošip and Grk on Korčula, Bogdanuša on Hvar, Vugava on Vis, Maraština, Debit and Kujundžuša, and, in Istria, Malvazija Istarska, the region's emblem, along with the red Teran.

Inland, Slavonia's Graševina is the country's most planted grape. It is made fresh, oak-aged or botrytised from the hills of the 'Golden Valley' around Kutjevo, where Cistercian monks built a cellar in 1232. On the Danube, Ilok's Traminac (Gewürztraminer) has royal glamour: its 1947 vintage is said to have been served at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953. Northern hills around Zagreb (Plešivica, Zagorje and Međimurje) make some of the country's best sparkling wines and crisp aromatic whites.

history.title: Greeks on Vis and Hvar
history.text: Greek colonists from Syracuse and Paros founded Issa (Vis) and Pharos (Stari Grad on Hvar, 384 BC). Pharos's field system, divided into parcels with stone walls and still planted with vines and olives, became the UNESCO Stari Grad Plain.

history.title: Cistercians at Kutjevo
history.text: Cistercian monks founded an abbey in the Požega valley and built the Kutjevo cellar in 1232; the valley's later name, Vallis Aurea (Golden Valley), reflects its farming wealth.

history.title: Tribidrag in the archives
history.text: A record of 1444 mentions the grape Tribidrag in Dalmatia; the Statute of Budva (1426 to 1442) had already named Cratosia (Kratošija). DNA later showed both are the variety now called Zinfandel.

history.title: Ilok's Old Cellar
history.text: Iločki podrumi dates its Old Cellar to 1450, under the Iločki (Újlaki) family; after the Ottoman era Ilok passed to the Odescalchi princes in 1697.

history.title: A Traminer for the Queen
history.text: Ilok's 1947 Traminac was reportedly served at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, a story the winery and the British Embassy still tell.

history.title: Dingač protected
history.text: Dingač on Pelješac became the first protected Croatian wine region; Postup followed in 1967, and in 1964 Dingač received international protection as a 'famous wine'.

history.title: The Dingač tunnel
history.text: On 29 November 1975 a 400 m tunnel through the Pelješac ridge opened, financed by the growers' cooperative, replacing donkey paths over the pass and cutting a 20 km detour to 4 km.

history.title: War on the Danube
history.text: The Croatian War of Independence devastated eastern Slavonia; Ilok was occupied and its cellars looted, and many Danube vineyards were mined or abandoned until reintegration in 1998.

history.title: Zinfandel found at Kaštela
history.text: Nine vines of Crljenak Kaštelanski in a vineyard at Kaštel Novi near Split matched Zinfandel's DNA, ending a decades-long search for the grape's European origin.

history.title: EU entry
history.text: Croatia joined the EU on 1 July 2013 and its wine PDOs were registered the same day; Ponikve (2021) and Muškat momjanski (2021) followed.

countries.classification: Croatian wine law nests regions (*regije*), subregions (*podregije*), vineyard areas (*vinogorja*) and single positions (*položaji*). Under the EU system 18 names are PDOs (*zaštićena oznaka izvornosti*, ZOI): the regions Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska, Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska and Primorska Hrvatska; the subregions Hrvatsko Podunavlje, Slavonija, Moslavina, Prigorje-Bilogora, Plešivica, Pokuplje, Zagorje-Međimurje, Hrvatska Istra, Hrvatsko primorje, Sjeverna Dalmacija, Srednja i Južna Dalmacija and Dalmatinska zagora; and the site appellations Dingač, Ponikve and Muškat momjanski. Labels still use the traditional quality terms *kvalitetno vino* (quality wine) and *vrhunsko vino* (premium wine), and Prädikat-style sweet categories (*kasna berba*, *izborna berba*, *izborna berba bobica*, *izborna berba prosušenih bobica*, *ledeno vino*). Prošek, the Dalmatian dried-grape dessert wine, is a traditional term whose EU protection Croatia sought from 2021, against Italian objections that it is too close to Prosecco.
countries.climate_soils: The coast is Mediterranean with hot, dry summers and mild winters; the bura (bora) and jugo winds shape it, and the steepest Dalmatian slopes get reflected light from the sea. Soils are karst limestone and dolomite, terra rossa in Istria, flysch (white marl, *bijela zemlja*) in northern Istria, and sand on islands such as Korčula's Lumbarda. Inland the climate is continental; Slavonia's hills are loess, clay and marl on the Papuk, Krndija and Psunj ranges, and the Danube terraces at Ilok and Erdut are thick loess.

grapes.name: Plavac Mali
grapes.note: The main Dalmatian red, offspring of Tribidrag (Zinfandel) and Dobričić; huge, tannic, high-alcohol wines on Pelješac, Hvar and Brač.

grapes.name: Crljenak Kaštelanski / Tribidrag
grapes.note: Zinfandel/Primitivo, rediscovered at Kaštela in 2001 and now replanted along the coast.

grapes.name: Graševina
grapes.note: Welschriesling, the most planted variety, especially in Slavonia; from fresh to botrytised.

grapes.name: Malvazija Istarska
grapes.note: Istria's white emblem: saline, peachy, made fresh, oak-aged or macerated.

grapes.name: Teran
grapes.note: Istrian red with high acidity and dark fruit, close to but distinct from Slovenia's Refošk-based Teran.

grapes.name: Pošip
grapes.note: Full-bodied white from Smokvica and Čara on Korčula; Pošip Čara is often cited as the first Croatian white with protected origin.

grapes.name: Grk
grapes.note: Female-flowering white of Lumbarda on Korčula's sands, interplanted with Plavac Mali as a pollinator.

grapes.name: Babić
grapes.note: Red of Primošten and Šibenik, grown in stone-walled micro-plots on bare rock.

grapes.name: Bogdanuša, Vugava, Maraština, Debit, Kujundžuša
grapes.note: Island and hinterland whites: Hvar, Vis, the Dalmatian coast and Imotski respectively.

grapes.name: Traminac
grapes.note: Gewürztraminer, famous at Ilok and in the Danube region.

grapes.name: Škrlet
grapes.note: Moslavina's native, light, citrusy white.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.tagline: Prokupac and Tamjanika, Fruška Gora's monastery slopes and Bermet, and the stone cellar towns of Negotin.

stats.note: Statistical Office of Serbia via the Netherlands agricultural attaché (2020): 20,406 ha of vineyard in 2018 and 331,000 hl of wine. Other sources give 22,150 ha, of which about 6,700 ha are registered for wine. Recent official figures were not found.

countries.overview:
Serbia was once the engine of Yugoslav wine. In the 1970s Yugoslavia made over 6 million hl a year, much of it in Serbian combines such as Navip and Rubin. Today's Serbian industry is far smaller but far more interesting. It has about 20,000 ha of vines, fewer than half registered for wine, and some 350 to 400 registered wineries, most of them family businesses founded after 2000. Production is roughly 0.3 to 0.4 million hl, and imports (above all from North Macedonia) exceed exports.

Serbian law divides the vineyard into three wine-growing units (Central Serbia, Vojvodina, and Kosovo and Metohija, a unit Serbia still defines for Kosovo although Kosovo has administered itself since 1999 and declared independence in 2008), 22 regions and 77 districts, under a zoning adopted in 2015 to match the EU's PDO and PGI system. Under the UK-Serbia trade agreement, 81 Serbian wine names are protected as geographical indications, from the large Šumadija-Velika Morava to small names such as Oplenac, Župa, Rajac and Palić.

The best-known areas are Fruška Gora, a low wooded ridge above the Danube near Novi Sad, studded with sixteen Orthodox monasteries and home to the herbal dessert wine Bermet of Sremski Karlovci; Vršac in the Banat, on the slopes of the only real hills of the Serbian Banat; Šumadija in the centre, with the royal Oplenac winery; Župa around Aleksandrovac, Serbia's 'wine capital', in the warm valley of the Rasina; and the Negotin Krajina and Timok in the east, where villages of stone cellars (*pivnice*) stand apart from the houses.

Two native grapes carry the story. Prokupac, an ancient red associated with the medieval Nemanjić dynasty, makes light-coloured, spicy, cherry-fruited reds; once dismissed as rustic, it is now the focus of a quality revival. Tamjanika, a local name for Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains grown in Serbia for centuries, makes intensely perfumed dry whites. Smederevka, Sremska Zelenika, Bagrina and the Hungarian-Serb Kadarka add more local colour, but international varieties dominate plantings.

history.title: Probus and Sirmium
history.text: The Roman emperor Probus, born at Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) in 232, is credited with lifting Domitian's limits on provincial vineyards and planting vines on Fruška Gora and the slopes above the Danube.

history.title: Nemanjić monasteries and vineyards
history.text: The Nemanjić dynasty and its monasteries promoted viticulture; monastic charters list vineyards in Župa, Metohija and the Morava valley. Legend says Prince Lazar gave his army communion with Župa wine before the Battle of Kosovo in 1389.

history.title: Habsburg Srem and Banat
history.text: After the Great Serbian Migration of 1690, Serbs settled in Habsburg Srem and Banat. Sremski Karlovci became the seat of the Serbian Orthodox metropolitan and a wine town, and Bermet became a court favourite.

history.title: Negotin's cellar towns
history.text: Vlach and Serbian winegrowers of the Negotin Krajina built separate cellar villages (pivnice) at Rajac, Rogljevo and Štubik. About 196 cellars survive. During the phylloxera crisis Negotin's wine was sold to France.

history.title: King Alexander's winery at Oplenac
history.text: King Alexander I built the King's Winery at the foot of Oplenac hill in Topola in 1931, planting over 50 ha with French and local varieties near the Karađorđević mausoleum.

history.title: Župa harvest festival
history.text: Aleksandrovac began holding the Župska berba harvest festival in 1963. It now draws hundreds of thousands of visitors each September.

history.title: Collapse and private revival
history.text: The breakup of Yugoslavia and sanctions crippled the state combines. After 2000 small private wineries multiplied, and a 2015 zoning adopted the EU geographical-indication model.

countries.classification: Serbia's wine law defines wines with geographical origin in three tiers: *kontrolisano poreklo* (KP, controlled origin), *kontrolisano poreklo i kvalitet* (KPK, controlled origin and quality) and *kontrolisano poreklo i garantovan kvalitet* (KPGK, controlled origin and guaranteed quality). These terms are registered as traditional terms under Serbia's agreements with the EU and UK. The 2015 zoning sets three wine-growing units, 22 regions (*rejoni*) and 77 districts (*vinogorja*). Under the UK-Serbia Partnership, Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) 81 Serbian wine names are protected as PGIs. Other traditional terms include *kasna berba* (late harvest), *suvarak* (dried-grape wine), *arhivsko vino* (archive wine) and *mlado vino* (young wine).
countries.climate_soils: Vojvodina in the north is flat Pannonian plain, with vineyards on its few hills (Fruška Gora's loess and marl, the Vršac hills' loess and schist) and on sands (Subotica-Horgoš, Deliblato). Central Serbia is hilly continental country of river valleys (Morava, Rasina, Timok) with clay, loess and limestone. Summers are hot and winters cold, and autumns are generally dry.

grapes.name: Prokupac
grapes.note: Ancient native red, light in colour with sour cherry, pepper and herbs; at its best in Župa, Toplica and Niš; the focus of the quality revival.

grapes.name: Tamjanika
grapes.note: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains under its Serbian name, grown for more than 500 years; aromatic dry whites from Župa, Negotin and Šumadija.

grapes.name: Smederevka
grapes.note: Old neutral white, the base of everyday spritzers (špricer).

grapes.name: Sremska Zelenika
grapes.note: Rare green-skinned white of Fruška Gora, being revived.

grapes.name: Kreaca
grapes.note: Kriaca, the local white of the Banat and Vršac.

grapes.name: Bagrina
grapes.note: Pink-skinned native white of the Negotin Krajina.

grapes.name: Morava
grapes.note: A modern Serbian white crossing bred at Sremski Karlovci, becoming a signature of Fruška Gora.

grapes.name: Graševina and Riesling
grapes.note: Welschriesling and Rhine Riesling, mainstays of Vojvodina.

countries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
countries.tagline: Sun-baked Herzegovinian karst, mineral Žilavka and the 'empty barrel' Blatina, with monks still making wine at Tvrdoš.

stats.note: Officials reported 2,657 ha of wine grapes in the Federation of BiH in 2016 plus about 600 ha in Republika Srpska, and 177,400 hl of wine (as reported by Jancis Robinson); there is no vineyard register, so the figures are approximate.

countries.overview:
Almost all of Bosnia and Herzegovina's wine comes from Herzegovina, the hot, stony south that drains to the Adriatic along the Neretva. Summers can hit 40 °C, the soils are thin karst and terra rossa, and the scenery around Mostar, Čitluk, Međugorje, Ljubuški, Stolac and Trebinje looks more like Dalmatia than central Europe. About 3,000 ha are planted, worked by up to 11,000 households, most of whom make wine for themselves; around 50 producers are registered and perhaps 30 sell commercially.

Two native grapes make up 60 to 65 percent of the vineyard. Žilavka is a firm, mineral, apricot-and-almond white, said to have been the preferred wine of the Austro-Hungarian emperors after 1878. Blatina is a dark, soft red whose flowers are functionally female, so it must be interplanted with a pollinator such as Trnjak, Vranac or Alicante Bouschet; its nickname 'empty barrel' comes from the poor yields of bad flowering years. Vranac grows around Trebinje, Plavac Mali near the Croatian border.

Viticulture here goes back to the Illyrians and Romans, survived four centuries of Ottoman rule (when wine was mostly made by Christian communities and monasteries), and grew under Austro-Hungarian administration from 1878. In the socialist era households were limited to 100 litres of wine a year, and large cooperatives such as Hepok in Mostar dominated. The 1990s war set the industry back badly; since then family estates (Vinarija Čitluk, Podrumi Andrija, Vukoje, Tvrdoš, Nuić, Škegro, Brkić, Carski Vinogradi) have rebuilt it, and the Herzegovina Wine Route, opened in 2007, was relaunched in 2023. The country imports about five times more wine than it exports.

history.title: Vines in Roman Dalmatia
history.text: Herzegovina lay in the Roman province of Dalmatia; local tradition and archaeology link viticulture to the Illyrians and Romans more than 2,000 years ago.

history.title: Tvrdoš monastery cellar
history.text: The Serbian Orthodox monastery of Tvrdoš near Trebinje, founded in the late 15th or early 16th century, has a wine cellar dating to the 15th century; its monks still make Vranac and Žilavka.

history.title: Austro-Hungarian Herzegovina
history.text: Austro-Hungarian administration modernised viticulture around Mostar; Žilavka became a favourite at the imperial court, and land at Trebinje was part of Emperor Franz Joseph's personal vineyard.

history.title: War and the Wine Route
history.text: The war devastated vineyards and wineries; the Herzegovina Wine Route opened in 2007 and was relaunched in 2023.

countries.classification: Bosnia and Herzegovina is not in the EU, and no wine names from it appear in the EU or UK geographical-indication registers. Wine law is set separately by the two entities (the Federation and Republika Srpska), and the traditional names Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina are widely used on labels. A national vineyard register did not exist as of the last available reporting, so origin rules are loosely enforced.
countries.climate_soils: Herzegovina has a Mediterranean-influenced climate with very hot, dry summers, mild winters and high sunshine; soils are karst limestone with pockets of terra rossa and stony alluvium along the Neretva. Northern Bosnia is continental and has only scattered vineyards.

grapes.name: Žilavka
grapes.note: Native white of Herzegovina: firm, mineral, apricot and almond; the country's signature wine.

grapes.name: Blatina
grapes.note: Native red with female flowers that needs a pollinator; soft, dark-fruited; nicknamed 'empty barrel'.

grapes.name: Vranac
grapes.note: Montenegrin red grown around Trebinje and in eastern Herzegovina.

grapes.name: Trnjak
grapes.note: Local red often interplanted with Blatina.

countries.name: Montenegro
countries.tagline: Vranac country around Lake Skadar, the possible cradle of Zinfandel, and a wine cellar inside a Cold War aircraft tunnel.

stats.note: Wein.plus (2022): 2,825 ha of vineyard and 70,000 hl of wine; Wikipedia gives over 2,800 ha and 22,200 t of grapes in 2017.

countries.overview:
Montenegro is small (about 2,800 ha of vines, roughly 70,000 hl a year) but it punches above its weight because of two grapes and one company. The grapes are Vranac, a deep-coloured, tannic red that makes up most of the country's wine, and Kratošija, a local name for the variety the world knows as Zinfandel or Primitivo; geneticists now consider Montenegro the most likely home of that grape, whose name as 'Cratosia' appears in the medieval Statute of Budva (1426 to 1442). Krstač is the native white, and Žižak and Kadarun are rarer reds.

The company is Plantaže 13. jul, founded in 1963 and still state-controlled, which planted the Ćemovsko polje plain south-east of Podgorica in the 1970s and 1980s into a single vineyard of more than 2,300 ha and some 11 million vines, one of the largest in Europe. It makes about 17 million bottles a year, led by Vranac Pro Corde and Crnogorski Vranac, and ages its premium wines in Šipčanik, a 356 m tunnel more than 30 m underground that was built as part of a military airfield and converted to a cellar in 2007.

Most vineyards lie in the basin of Lake Skadar, where the hot Zeta plain and the terraced slopes of Crmnica around Virpazar catch both Adriatic and continental influences; the Boka Kotorska and Budva-Bar coast and the cooler north make the rest. A legal decision of 2017 defines four wine regions and 15 subregions in line with EU practice, in preparation for EU membership.

history.title: Cratosia in the Statute of Budva
history.text: The medieval Statute of Budva mentions a grape called Cratosia, probably today's Kratošija, the earliest known record of the variety later identified as Zinfandel/Primitivo.

history.title: King Nikola's revival
history.text: Under Prince (later King) Nikola I viticulture recovered after Ottoman-era losses; Crmnica wine won first prizes at the 1907 Balkan Exhibition in London.

history.title: Plantaže and Ćemovsko polje
history.text: Plantaže was founded in 1963 with its first cellar at Lješkopolje; the Ćemovsko polje cellar opened in 1981 with 190,000 hl of capacity.

history.title: Šipčanik
history.text: In November 2007 Plantaže began ageing wine in Šipčanik, a 356 m tunnel more than 30 m underground in a former military facility of the airfield under the vineyard.

history.title: Wine regions defined
history.text: A government decision of October 2017 defined four wine-production regions and fifteen subregions.

countries.classification: A 2017 government decision (Official Gazette 65/2017) defines four wine-production regions: the Montenegrin basin of Lake Skadar (subregions Kučki, Crmnički, Riječki, Podgorički, Piperski, Katunski, Bjelopavlićki), the Montenegrin coast (Boka Kotorska, Budva-Bar, Ulcinj, Adriatic hinterland), Nudo, and the Montenegrin north (Nikšićki, Bjelopoljski, Šćepan polje, Dragaljsko polje). No Montenegrin wine names were found in the EU or UK GI registers as of 2026.
countries.climate_soils: The Skadar basin is hot, with Mediterranean summers and karst-limestone soils, gravels and terra rossa on the Zeta plain; Crmnica's terraces get Adriatic air over the coastal mountains. The coast is Mediterranean and the north continental.

grapes.name: Vranac
grapes.note: The national red, over 70% of production: deep colour, high tannin, black fruit.

grapes.name: Kratošija
grapes.note: Montenegro's name for Tribidrag/Zinfandel/Primitivo; dominant before phylloxera, now being replanted.

grapes.name: Krstač
grapes.note: Native white of the Podgorica area.

grapes.name: Žižak and Kadarun
grapes.note: Rare local reds.

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.tagline: The Vardar valley's sun-soaked Vranec, the ruins of Stobi and the Balkans' biggest winery at Kavadarci.

stats.note: Wein.plus: 24,776 ha of wine vineyards and 854,000 hl of wine in 2022; GIZ (2026) expected 90 to 100 million litres in 2025, at least 85% exported.

countries.overview:
North Macedonia is a wine exporter first: in a normal year it makes 0.9 to 1 million hl and sends at least 85 percent abroad, much of it in bulk to Serbia, Croatia, Germany and beyond. In the 1980s it made about two-thirds of Yugoslavia's wine. The vineyard (about 25,000 ha for wine, plus large plantings of table grapes) is dominated by red grapes, about 80 percent, and above all by Vranec, with roughly 9,500 ha. Smederevka (Dimyat) is the main white.

Three regions organise the country: Povardarie, the Vardar valley from Skopje to the Greek border, with about 85 to 87 percent of vineyards and 90 percent of wineries; Pčinja-Osogovo in the east toward Bulgaria; and Pelagonija-Polog in the west, including Ohrid and Prespa. The heart of Povardarie is Tikveš, the basin around Kavadarci and Negotino, where hot summers (often over 35 °C), Mediterranean air funnelled up the Vardar from the Aegean and cold continental winters give dark, ripe, full-bodied reds. Tikveš winery in Kavadarci, which dates its history to 1885, is the largest in South-Eastern Europe; Stobi, Bovin, Popova Kula, Chateau Kamnik and Dalvina lead the newer estates.

Native grapes include Stanušina, a light, local red of Tikveš, and Kratošija (Tribidrag/Zinfandel). The ancient city of Stobi on the Vardar, with mosaics showing vines and wine, recalls that Paeonians, Macedonians and Romans all made wine here. Since 2024 amendments to the Wine Law have aimed to introduce EU-style geographical indications, and the first, 'Vardar Valley', was being prepared in 2026.

history.title: Stobi on the Vardar
history.text: Stobi, a Paeonian then Macedonian and Roman city at the confluence of the Crna and Vardar, has mosaics with vine and wine motifs; the Stobi winery nearby takes its name.

history.title: Tikveš winery
history.text: Tikveš winery in Kavadarci dates its founding to 1885; it became a cooperative after 1946 and was privatised with new investment in 2003. It is described as the largest winery in South-Eastern Europe.

history.title: Yugoslavia's vineyard
history.text: Macedonia produced about two-thirds of Yugoslav wine; output fell from about 1.8 million hl in the mid-1990s to 447,000 hl in 2002 after the federation broke up.

history.title: Toward geographical indications
history.text: Wine Law amendments in 2024 opened the way for EU-style GIs; 'Vardar Valley' was being prepared as the first, coordinated by the Povardarski wine region body.

countries.classification: North Macedonia has three wine regions (Povardarie, Pčinja-Osogovo, Pelagonija-Polog) subdivided into 16 to 18 wine areas (*vinogorja*) such as Tikveš, Skopje, Veles, Ovče Pole, Gevgelija-Valandovo, Strumica-Radoviš, Kočani-Vinica, Kratovo, Kumanovo, Prilep, Bitola, Ohrid, Prespa, Tetovo and Kičevo. Labels have long used 'controlled origin' wording tied to these areas. Wine Law amendments adopted in April 2024 set up an EU-compatible system of geographical indications; as of early 2026 the first GI, 'Vardar Valley', was in preparation. Note that the EU PGI 'Macedonia' refers to Greek Macedonia.
countries.climate_soils: The Vardar valley is a corridor of hot, dry summers and Mediterranean influence from the Aegean, with cold winters and frequent wind; soils are alluvial, sandy and clay-loam on terraces, with limestone and schist on the hills. The west (Ohrid, Prespa, Bitola) is higher and cooler.

grapes.name: Vranec
grapes.note: About 9,500 ha: the national red, dark and tannic, from rustic bulk wine to aged single-vineyard bottlings.

grapes.name: Smederevka
grapes.note: About 6,500 ha, the main white (Dimyat elsewhere).

grapes.name: Kratošija
grapes.note: About 1,000 ha of Tribidrag/Zinfandel.

grapes.name: Stanušina
grapes.note: Rare native red of Tikveš, light and fragrant.

grapes.name: Temjanika and Žilavka
grapes.note: Aromatic Muscat and Herzegovinian white grown in smaller amounts.

countries.name: Albania
countries.tagline: Kallmet, Shesh and Pulës: native grapes on the Adriatic hills, recovering from a century of upheaval.

stats.note: Wikipedia (national statistics): 10,178 ha of vineyard and 204,000 t of grapes in 2015; no reliable recent wine-production figure found.

countries.overview:
Albania has grown vines since the Illyrians, at least 3,000 years ago, and the Greek and Roman colonies of the coast (Apollonia, Dyrrhachium, Butrint) left wine imagery in their ruins. The Ottoman centuries reduced vineyards largely to Christian areas, phylloxera nearly destroyed what remained by 1933, and after 1945 the Communist regime planted collective vineyards (from about 2,700 ha after the war to over 17,000 ha by 1990) for brandy and bulk wine. The collapse of 1991 and the privatisation chaos that followed broke up those estates; today about 10,000 ha are planted, mostly for table grapes and home wine and raki, and a few dozen commercial wineries are building a modern identity.

That identity rests on native grapes. Kallmet, a red named after the village of Kallmet near Lezhë, grows on the Zadrima plain between Shkodër and Lezhë and makes dark, spicy wines. Shesh i Zi (black) and Shesh i Bardhë (white) take their name from Shesh, near Tirana, and are the most widespread. Pulës is a white of Berat, Debinë a white from the south-east (Korçë, Përmet), and Vlosh a red of the Vlorë coast. The best-known producers include Kantina Arbëri in Mirditë (Kallmet), Çobo near Berat (Pulës and Shesh), Kokomani near Tirana, Nurellari in Skrapar, Skënderbeu and Bardha.

Albania is an EU candidate. Under its trade agreement with the United Kingdom, 36 Albanian wine names, essentially its historic districts from Shkodër and Koplik to Korçë, Përmet, Berat and Sarandë, are protected as geographical indications.

history.title: Illyrian and Greek vines
history.text: Illyrian tribes and the Greek colonies of Epidamnos (Durrës) and Apollonia grew and traded wine; Roman Butrint's decorations show its importance.

history.title: Phylloxera
history.text: Phylloxera nearly wiped out Albanian viticulture; after the Second World War only about 2,737 ha remained.

history.title: Collective vineyards
history.text: The Communist state expanded vineyards to about 17,600 ha by 1990 for wine and brandy, but exports fell from 61,000 hl (1971) to 22,000 hl (1985).

history.title: Private revival
history.text: After 1991 collective farms were dismantled and family wineries emerged, focusing on Kallmet, Shesh, Pulës and Debinë.

countries.classification: Albania is not in the EU and has no EU-registered wine PDOs or PGIs. Under the UK-Albania trade agreement, 36 Albanian wine names are protected in the UK as geographical indications, corresponding to the country's historic districts (rrethe): Berat, Bulqizë, Delvinë, Devoll, Dibër, Durrës, Elbasan, Fier, Gjirokastër, Gramsh, Has, Kavajë, Kolonjë, Koplik, Korçë, Krujë, Kukës, Kurbin, Kuçovë, Lezhë, Librazhd, Lushnjë, Mallakastër, Mat, Mirditë, Peqin, Pogradec, Pukë, Përmet, Sarandë, Shkodër, Skrapar, Tepelenë, Tiranë, Tropojë and Vlorë.
countries.climate_soils: The coastal plain and hills are Mediterranean, with hot dry summers; the interior and the south-eastern highlands around Korçë are continental and cooler. Soils range from alluvial plains to limestone and flysch hills.

grapes.name: Kallmet
grapes.note: Native red of the Zadrima plain near Lezhë and Shkodër, named after the village of Kallmet.

grapes.name: Shesh i Zi and Shesh i Bardhë
grapes.note: Red and white grapes named after Shesh near Tirana; the most widespread natives.

grapes.name: Pulës
grapes.note: White grape of Berat.

grapes.name: Debinë
grapes.note: White of the south-east (Korçë, Përmet).

grapes.name: Vlosh
grapes.note: Red of the Vlorë coast.

countries.name: Kosovo
countries.tagline: The Rahovec valley's sunny slopes, once the source of a German supermarket red, rebuilding as a small wine country.

stats.note: Kosovo Ministry of Industry, Entrepreneurship and Trade: 3,405.54 ha of vineyard in 2024 (Rahovec 2,465 ha, Suharekë 575, Prizren 198, Gjakovë 77, Malishevë 65); 35 licensed wineries, three of which make about 70% of the wine.

countries.overview:
Kosovo's vineyards are concentrated in the south-west, in the Dukagjin plain (Rrafshi i Dukagjinit) and especially around Rahovec (Orahovac in Serbian), which alone has about 2,465 of the country's 3,400 ha. The hills around Rahovec, at 300 to 600 m with around 276 sunny days a year, loamy and red soils and a ripening season from mid-July to mid-October, have grown grapes since antiquity. In the Yugoslav era the state winery at Rahovec shipped large volumes of soft red wine to West Germany; it was sold there under brands such as Amselfelder, German for 'blackbird field', the meaning of the Serbian name Kosovo Polje.

War in 1998 and 1999 and the loss of the German market left the sector in ruins. The old state winery was privatised in 2006 as Stone Castle, bought for €5.5 million by Albanian-American businessman Rrustem Gecaj; it has a capacity of 10 to 13 million litres and is one of the largest private wineries in the region. Today 35 licensed wineries operate, three of them making about 70 percent of the wine, alongside many small family cellars in Rahovec, Suharekë and Prizren. Main grapes include Vranac, Prokupac, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Smederevka, Riesling and Chardonnay.

history.title: Rahovec's big winery
history.text: The Rahovec winery that became Stone Castle was founded in 1952; it grew into a major exporter of red wine to West Germany in the Yugoslav period.

history.title: War
history.text: The Kosovo war devastated vineyards and ended the German export trade.

history.title: Stone Castle privatised
history.text: The former state winery was privatised for €5.5 million and renamed Stone Castle; its capacity is 10 to 13 million litres.

countries.classification: Kosovo regulates wine through its own wine law and a register of licensed producers; vineyard statistics are kept by region (Rahovec, Suharekë, Prizren, Gjakovë, Malishevë). No Kosovar wine names appear in the EU or UK geographical-indication registers as of 2026.
countries.climate_soils: Continental with Mediterranean influence from the south-west; about 276 sunny days a year in Rahovec; loamy soils with some red soils; vineyards mostly at 300 to 600 m.

grapes.name: Vranac and Prokupac
grapes.note: Balkan reds that dominate the local blends.

grapes.name: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: International reds planted widely in the Yugoslav era.

grapes.name: Smederevka, Riesling, Chardonnay, Žilavka
grapes.note: Main whites.

countries.name: Romania
countries.tagline: Europe's sixth vineyard, ringed by the Carpathians: Fetească in three colours, botrytised Grasă at Cotnari and the Black Sea warmth of Murfatlar.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025: 187 kha of vineyard (all grape uses), 3.3 mhl produced in 2025 (13th in the production table), 17.6% below the five-year average. Eurostat counts 162 kha of wine-grape vines for 2025.

countries.overview:
Romania has the biggest vineyard in Central and Eastern Europe: about 187,000 ha in 2025 according to the OIV, the fourth largest in the EU after Spain, France and Italy. In 2025 it made 3.3 million hl of wine, a small crop by its own standards after spring frosts, hail and drought in the west. The shape of the country explains its wine. The Carpathian arc curls through the middle like a horseshoe, and almost every important vineyard sits on its outer or inner foothills: the long eastern and southern flanks in Moldavia and Muntenia, the Transylvanian plateau inside the arc, and the western hills facing Hungary and Serbia. Beyond the mountains lie the Danube terraces, sandy southern plains, and Dobrogea between the Danube and the Black Sea.

The law groups this into eight viticultural regions and, under the EU system, 33 DOCs (*denumire de origine controlată*, PDO) and 12 IGs (PGI). The DOCs range from big hill districts such as Dealu Mare, Târnave, Odobești and Panciu to tiny ones like Pietroasa, Adamclisi and Însurăței. DOC wines can carry a ripeness level: DOC-CMD (harvested at full maturity), DOC-CT (late harvest) and DOC-CIB (noble-berry selection, botrytised).

The native grapes are the reason to explore. Fetească Neagră ('black maiden') is the country's signature red, plummy and spicy, at its best in Dealu Mare. Fetească Albă and Fetească Regală, the latter a natural cross that appeared in Transylvania around 1920, are the main whites. Tămâioasă Românească (a Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains) and the pink-skinned Busuioacă de Bohotin make aromatic dry and sweet wines. Grasă de Cotnari, the same grape as Tokaj's Kövérszőlő, makes botrytised sweet wines at Cotnari that rivalled Tokaji in the 19th century. Băbească Neagră, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac, Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Galbenă de Odobești, Frâncușă and Șarba fill in the local map.

History has whipsawed the industry. Strabo wrote that the Dacian king Burebista ordered vines destroyed; medieval princes such as Stephen the Great endowed monasteries and vineyards; phylloxera, first found at Chitorani in Dealu Mare in the 1880s, forced replanting with French varieties; and the Communist state turned Romania into a bulk supplier for the Soviet bloc, with 80 to 90 percent of output exported in some periods. Since 1989, and especially since EU entry in 2007, investment from Romanian entrepreneurs and foreign partners has modernised wineries such as Cramele Recaș, Jidvei, Prince Știrbey, Davino, LacertA, Avincis, Crama Oprișor, Liliac, Corcova and Bauer. A large share of production is still semi-sweet and sold domestically, but the best dry wines, especially Fetească Neagră and the aromatic whites, are well worth finding.

history.title: Burebista's vine purge
history.text: The Greek geographer Strabo wrote that Burebista, king of the Dacians, on the advice of the priest Decaeneus, ordered vineyards destroyed to keep his warriors sober. Romanian historians regard the passage as exaggerated, but it is the oldest anecdote about wine in the region.

history.title: Greek colonies on the Black Sea
history.text: Greek colonies at Histria, Tomis (Constanța) and Callatis (Mangalia) traded wine and planted vines in Dobrogea, the start of the Murfatlar tradition.

history.title: Roman Dacia
history.text: After Trajan's conquest Roman colonists spread viticulture across Transylvania and Oltenia; the Tropaeum Traiani monument at Adamclisi commemorates the conquest.

history.title: Stephen the Great and Cotnari
history.text: The Moldavian prince Stephen the Great expanded the Cotnari vineyards and court cellars; Grasă de Cotnari has been grown there since his reign.

history.title: Despot Vodă's Latin school
history.text: Prince Despot Vodă founded a Latin school (Schola Latina) at Cotnari in 1562, a sign of the town's wealth from wine; Cotnari reached its peak under him and Stephen the Great.

history.title: Phylloxera at Chitorani
history.text: Phylloxera was first recorded in Romania at Chitorani in Dealu Mare and devastated local viticulture over the following years; replanting through the early 20th century used grafted French varieties.

history.title: Research and Fetească Regală
history.text: The research station at Valea Călugărească and the discovery of Fetească Regală at Daneș in Transylvania around 1920 shaped modern Romanian vine growing.

history.title: State farms and export
history.text: Communist central planning merged estates into state farms (IAS) and cooperatives; up to 80 to 90 percent of wine was exported, much of it to the Soviet Union.

history.title: Privatisation and EU entry
history.text: Land restitution fragmented vineyards; foreign and domestic investors rebuilt wineries, and Romania joined the EU in 2007, registering its DOCs the same year.

countries.classification:
Romanian wine law follows the EU: 33 DOCs (*denumire de origine controlată*, the Romanian name for a PDO) and 12 IGs (*indicație geografică*, PGI), plus wine without origin. Several DOCs list sub-denominations that can appear on labels (for example Dealu Mare-Urlați, Dealu Mare-Valea Călugărească, Murfatlar-Medgidia, Târnave-Jidvei). DOC wines may also carry a ripeness level:
- DOC-CMD (*cules la maturitate deplină*): full ripeness, at least 187 g/l of sugar at harvest
- DOC-CT (*cules târziu*): late harvest, at least 220 g/l
- DOC-CIB (*cules la înnobilarea boabelor*): botrytised berry selection, at least 240 g/l

The national body ONVPV (Oficiul Național al Viei și Produselor Vitivinicole) manages registration and control. Adamclisi (2020) and Însurăței (2018) are the newest DOCs.
countries.climate_soils: The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters; the Carpathians shelter the eastern and southern foothills from cold air, and the Black Sea moderates Dobrogea, the sunniest and driest part of the country. Soils range from the chernozem and loess-covered hills of Moldavia and Muntenia, the marls and clays of Transylvania and the limestone and loess of Dobrogea to the sand dunes of Oltenia's southern plain (Sadova-Corabia).

grapes.name: Fetească Neagră
grapes.note: The signature native red: plum, black cherry and spice; best in Dealu Mare, Dobrogea and Moldavia.

grapes.name: Fetească Regală
grapes.note: The most planted native white, a natural cross of Fetească Albă and Frâncușă first noted at Daneș around 1920; crisp, floral, often sparkling.

grapes.name: Fetească Albă
grapes.note: Old Moldavian and Transylvanian white, softer and more aromatic.

grapes.name: Tămâioasă Românească
grapes.note: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, famous for sweet wines at Pietroasa and Cotnari.

grapes.name: Grasă de Cotnari
grapes.note: Botrytis-prone white, identical to Tokaj's Kövérszőlő; sweet wines with up to about 300 g/l of sugar.

grapes.name: Băbească Neagră
grapes.note: Light, sour-cherry red of southern Moldavia (Nicorești, Dealu Bujorului).

grapes.name: Busuioacă de Bohotin
grapes.note: Pink-skinned Muscat with basil-like aromatics, from Bohotin near Iași.

grapes.name: Crâmpoșie Selecționată
grapes.note: Crisp white of Drăgășani, a selection of the old Crâmpoșie.

grapes.name: Negru de Drăgășani and Novac
grapes.note: Red crossings bred at Drăgășani in the 1990s from local and international parents.

grapes.name: Galbenă de Odobești, Frâncușă, Șarba
grapes.note: Local whites of Vrancea and Moldavia; Șarba is aromatic, Galbenă tart.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.tagline: Dionysus's homeland, the Cabernet that taught Britain to drink red, and native grapes such as Mavrud and Broadleaf Melnik finding their voice again.

stats.note: Vineyard area: OIV 2025 (58 kha). Production: 66 million litres in 2025 according to the Executive Agency for Vine and Wine (BTA, 2026), 10 to 15% below 2024; OIV reported 712,000 hl for 2024.

countries.overview:
Bulgaria sits on one of the oldest wine soils in Europe. The Thracians, who held these lands from the second millennium BC to late antiquity, worshipped a wine god the Greeks later knew as Dionysus, poured libations from gold rhyta and built rock sanctuaries such as Perperikon and the mound temples of Starosel. Archaeologists trace grape growing in the Thracian valley back several thousand years. Two mountain ranges organise the country: the Balkan range (Stara Planina) runs east to west through the middle and splits a continental north from a warmer south, and the Rhodope and Pirin massifs close off the south and south-west.

The modern map has five traditional regions: the Danubian Plain in the north, the Black Sea coast in the east, the Sub-Balkan valley of the Rose Valley beneath the Balkan range, the Thracian Lowlands in the south and the Struma valley in the south-west. Two large PGIs, Thracian Lowlands and Danube Plain, are what most labels actually use. There are also 52 PDOs, a legacy of the socialist-era control system, most named after a town and its old state winery. Critics note that so many PDOs mean little to drinkers, and few producers use them.

The OIV counted about 58,000 ha of vineyard in 2025, down from 145,000 ha at the end of the Second World War. In 2025 the 365 operating wineries (151 with foreign investors) made about 66 million litres, a short crop, while Bulgarians drink 110 to 120 million litres a year. International grapes dominate, roughly 70 percent of the vineyard, but the native varieties carry the interest. Mavrud from Asenovgrad and Perushtitsa makes deep, tannic, blackberry-and-spice reds. Shiroka Melnishka Loza (Broadleaf Melnik) is the late-ripening red of the Struma valley around Melnik, and its offspring Ranna Melnishka Loza (Melnik 55) ripens earlier. Rubin, a 1944 Nebbiolo x Syrah cross from Pleven, makes dark, fragrant reds. Gamza (Kadarka) is the light, peppery red of the north-west. Pamid is the old everyday red. Dimyat, a Gouais Blanc offspring, is the Black Sea white, and Misket Cherven (Red Misket) is grown around Sungurlare and Karlovo.

The modern story turns on one export miracle. In the 1970s and 1980s the state export monopoly Vinimpex sold soft, cheap Bulgarian Cabernet Sauvignon to British supermarkets and off-licences. Exports to the UK passed 2 million cases in 1990 and reached 3.3 million by 1994. The collapse after 1989 (slow land restitution, privatisation fights, neglected vineyards) erased that position by the late 1990s. Since EU entry in 2007 a new generation of estates has rebuilt quality, among them Bessa Valley, Castra Rubra, Katarzyna, Terra Tangra, Zagreus, Rumelia, Villa Melnik, Logodaj, Bononia, Burgozone, Tipchenitza and Midalidare.

history.title: Starosel's Thracian temples
history.text: The mound temple of Chetinyova Mogila near Starosel, dated to the late 5th and early 4th centuries BC and excavated from 2000, is the largest of several Thracian cult complexes in the area, now the backdrop to a winery.

history.title: Perperikon, sanctuary of Dionysus
history.text: On a 470 m rock hill near Kardzhali, Perperikon was a sacred site from prehistory to the Middle Ages; a famous temple of Dionysus is thought to have stood here. Excavations by Nikolay Ovcharov began in 2000.

history.title: The Panagyurishte gold
history.text: The Panagyurishte treasure, found in 1949, includes gold rhyta and a phiale used for wine at Thracian feasts, among the finest drinking vessels to survive from antiquity.

history.title: Khan Krum's decree
history.text: Legend says the Bulgarian ruler Khan Krum ordered the vineyards uprooted to curb drunkenness, and that a young man named Mavrud, emboldened by wine, killed a lion, which persuaded Krum to relent and gave the Mavrud grape its name. Like Burebista's Dacian edict, it is more legend than record.

history.title: Kordopulov House, Melnik
history.text: A merchant's house with a rock-cut cellar able to hold about 300 tonnes of wine was built in Melnik in 1754 and later bought by the Greek wine trader Manolis Kordopoulos, who shipped Melnik wine across Europe.

history.title: Liberation and phylloxera
history.text: After liberation from the Ottomans the vineyard grew to about 100,000 ha before phylloxera arrived; by the 1920s only about 45,000 ha remained.

history.title: Breeding new grapes
history.text: Rubin (Nebbiolo x Syrah) was created at the Pleven institute in 1944; Ranna Melnishka Loza (Melnik 55) was bred at Sandanski in 1963 from Shiroka Melnishka Loza, with Valdiguié later identified by DNA as the pollen parent.

history.title: Five regions decreed
history.text: A government decree of 13 July 1960 divided Bulgaria into five viticultural regions, the framework still used informally today.

history.title: The British Cabernet boom
history.text: Bulgarian Cabernet Sauvignon became a staple of UK supermarkets; exports to Britain topped 2 million cases in 1990 and reached 3.3 million in 1994 before collapsing as privatisation and land restitution stalled.

history.title: EU entry
history.text: Bulgaria joined the EU and its 52 PDOs and two PGIs were registered; foreign investment followed, and by 2026 151 of 365 wineries had foreign investors.

countries.classification: Under EU rules Bulgaria has 52 PDOs (*защитено наименование за произход*, ZNP) and two PGIs (*защитено географско указание*): Тракийска низина (Thracian Lowlands) and Дунавска равнина (Danube Plain). The PDOs, registered in 2007 (Bolyarovo in 2009), are mostly named after a town and its surrounding municipalities, inherited from the socialist-era Controliran (DGO/DGOC) system; most serious producers prefer the two PGIs, which are flexible and widely recognised. The Executive Agency for Vine and Wine (IAVV) supervises the system. Traditional terms include *резерва* (reserve), *специална резерва* and *премиум*.
countries.climate_soils: North of the Balkan range the Danubian Plain is temperate continental with hot summers and cold winters, on chernozem and loess. The Black Sea coast is milder and humid, good for whites. The Thracian Lowlands south of the Balkan range are warmer and drier, with Mediterranean influence moving up the Maritsa valley. Soils there are cinnamon forest soils, smolnitsa (black clay) and alluvium. The Struma valley in the south-west is the warmest corner, almost Mediterranean, with sandstone and sandy soils around Melnik.

grapes.name: Mavrud
grapes.note: Late, low-yielding native red of Asenovgrad and Perushtitsa (about 2% of plantings): dark, tannic, blackberry and spice.

grapes.name: Shiroka Melnishka Loza
grapes.note: Broadleaf Melnik, endemic to the Struma valley around Melnik; late-ripening, spicy, oak-friendly; reportedly Winston Churchill's favourite Bulgarian wine.

grapes.name: Ranna Melnishka Loza (Melnik 55)
grapes.note: Early Melnik, bred at Sandanski in 1963 from Broadleaf Melnik and Valdiguié; riper, rounder and easier.

grapes.name: Rubin
grapes.note: Nebbiolo x Syrah cross from Pleven (1944): deep colour, violet perfume, firm structure.

grapes.name: Gamza
grapes.note: Kadarka, the light, peppery red of the north-west Danube plain (Vidin, Suhindol, Pavlikeni).

grapes.name: Pamid
grapes.note: Old, light, low-acid native red, once the most planted grape in the country.

grapes.name: Dimyat
grapes.note: Black Sea white, offspring of Gouais Blanc; fresh, floral, also used for brandy.

grapes.name: Misket Cherven
grapes.note: Red Misket, a pink-skinned aromatic white of Sungurlare and the Rose Valley.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
grapes.note: The backbone of the 1980s export boom and still the most planted reds.
