regions.name: Tokaj
regions.tagline: Twenty-seven villages, a cone of volcanic hills and two rivers that breathe fog: the place that turned noble rot into a royal drink.
regions.summary:
Tokaj (in Hungarian usage also Tokaj-Hegyalja, 'Tokaj foothills') is a crescent of about 400 extinct volcanic hills at the southern tip of the Zemplén Mountains in north-eastern Hungary. It runs some 80 km from Abaújszántó in the west to Sátoraljaújhely on the Slovak border, with the town of Tokaj at its southern point where the Bodrog meets the Tisza. The protected area covers 27 settlements; within them only land ranked Class I or II in the vineyard cadastre may grow Tokaji. Roughly 5,500 ha are planted, out of more than 11,000 ha classified as vineyard land, and a small Slovak corner (seven villages, about 900 ha) shares the history and, since a 2004 agreement, a version of the name.

Everything here starts with *Botrytis cinerea*. In a good autumn the river fogs of the Bodrog and Tisza hang over the lower slopes in the morning, and dry, warm afternoons follow. The rot pierces Furmint and Hárslevelű skins, the berries shrivel into raisins called *aszú* and concentrate sugar and acid together. Pickers go through the rows several times and collect these berries one by one. Steeped in fermenting must or young wine and then aged for years in small casks in cellars cut into rock, they become Tokaji Aszú: amber, honeyed, apricot and orange peel, marmalade and tea, but always held up by Furmint's electric acidity, so the wine tastes alive rather than cloying.

Since the 1990s Tokaj has learned a second language: dry. Single-vineyard dry Furmint from sites such as Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Mézes Mály or Lapis now shows the same volcanic intensity in a form you can drink with dinner, and the region's 400-plus named dűlők are being mapped and bottled one by one. The sweet styles remain the crown jewels: Eszencia, the barely fermented free-run syrup of aszú berries; Aszú itself; Szamorodni, the 'as it comes' wine made from whole bunches with whatever rot they carry, dry and nutty under a film of yeast or sweet; and the old by-products Fordítás and Máslás.

For a visitor the region reads like a ring road of villages, each with its hill. Tokaj and Tarcal sit on Tokaj hill (Kopasz-hegy, 514 m) with its loess-covered southern face. Mád and its neighbours Rátka, Tállya and Mezőzombor hold the densest cluster of historic first growths. Bodrogkeresztúr, Bodrogkisfalud, Szegi and Olaszliszka line the Bodrog. Erdőbénye in the forested north was a coopering town, Tolcsva is home to Oremus and the old state winery, and Sárospatak and Sátoraljaújhely in the north-east hold the Rákóczi castle, the Megyer and Pajzos vineyards and the Oremus hill itself.
regions.history:
Vines were documented around Tokaj by the 12th century, and after the Tatar invasion of 1241 Béla IV brought in 'Latin' settlers (Walloons and Italians) whose memory lingers in Olaszliszka and Bodrogolaszi. In the 16th century Ottoman pressure on the southern wine regions, especially Szerémség (Syrmia), pushed vinedressers north; tradition holds that Szerémség growers who settled in Hegyalja around 1524 brought botrytised-wine know-how with them. The earliest firm written reference to aszú wine is the 1571 inheritance letter of Máté Garai, found by István Zelenák in 2002; Szikszai Fabricius's dictionary of 1576 records the term too. Máslás, a by-product of aszú making, is already mentioned in 1561, which suggests aszú was older still.

The famous story credits Máté Szepsi Laczkó (c. 1576 to 1632/33), a Reformed pastor at Erdőbénye and chaplain to Zsuzsanna Lorántffy, wife of Prince György I Rákóczi, with the first aszú: made in 1631 (some say 1630) from grapes of the Oremus vineyard at Sátoraljaújhely and served at Easter. The legend is attractive and almost certainly untrue in its claim of invention; his own chronicle never mentions aszú, and the town book in which it was supposedly recorded has never been found. What is true is that the Rákóczi princes, who owned castles at Sárospatak and Szerencs and great vineyard estates in the hills, turned Tokaji into an instrument of statecraft. In 1641 the towns of Hegyalja adopted a 48-point code regulating vineyard work and winemaking, and in 1655 the tithe on aszú grapes was abolished, encouraging growers to pick botrytised berries separately.

The golden age followed. Ferenc II Rákóczi, leader of the 1703 to 1711 war of independence, sent Tokaji to Louis XIV, and the line 'Vinum Regum, Rex Vinorum' entered legend. Peter the Great and his successors kept a Russian purchasing commission in Tokaj from 1733 to 1798; Polish merchants carried the wine north and gave Szamorodni its name. Vineyards were ranked into first, second and third classes from the 1720s (János Matolai's survey published by Mátyás Bél) and the work was completed by the censuses of 1765 and 1772; Antal Szirmay refined the ranking in 1798. On 1 October 1737 King Charles VI decreed which settlements could sell wine as Tokaji and required permission to plant, creating a closed production district more than a century before any similar law elsewhere. The finest Eszencia was reserved for the Habsburg cellars; as late as 1900 Franz Joseph sent Queen Victoria 972 bottles of Aszú for her birthday, and Hungary's national anthem (1823) thanks God for the 'nectar dripping from the vine-shoots of Tokaj'.

Then decline. Phylloxera arrived in 1885. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon put the north-eastern corner into Czechoslovakia. After 1945 the land was collectivised and a state combine (the Tokajhegyaljai Állami Gazdasági Borkombinát, later Tokaj Kereskedőház) bought grapes from thousands of smallholders and controlled bottling and export. Volume and oxidative, sometimes fortified styles replaced site and care. In 1990 the gate reopened. Hugh Johnson, the Danish winemaker Peter Vinding-Diers and around 60 Hungarian growers founded Royal Tokaji at Mád; AXA bought Disznókő in 1992; the Álvarez family of Vega Sicilia founded Oremus at Tolcsva in 1993; French groups took over Hétszőlő, Pajzos and Megyer. István Szepsy's low-yield aszú (released from 1991) and his 2000-vintage dry wines, made in part with Zoltán Demeter at Királyudvar, showed what the hills could do. UNESCO inscribed the Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape in 2002, Hungary won sole use of 'Tokaj' in the EU on accession (the Italian Tocai and Alsace Tokay names were retired by 2007), and in 2013 the region rewrote its rules to put minimum quality above tradition.
regions.terroir:
Tokaj sits at about 48°N, at the edge where the Zemplén volcanic range drops onto the Great Plain. Miocene eruptions some 12 to 15 million years ago left rhyolite, andesite and dacite, interleaved with layered tuffs, and their weathering gives the heavy, iron-red clay called *nyirok* and the white, porous *kaolin* and pumice-rich soils of Mád and Erdőbénye. Some sites carry zeolite, a volcanic mineral that holds water and nutrients; quartz-rich hydrothermal rock (the *kovás*, or flint-like, quartzite) caps hills like Úrágya and Szent Tamás. About 5% of the region, mostly on the southern face of Tokaj hill around Tarcal and Tokaj, is covered with loess, which warms faster in spring and gives rounder, earlier-ripening wines with a soft, fine texture. Hungarian growers talk of 'nyirok wines' (tense, smoky, long-lived) versus 'loess wines' (perfumed and supple).

The climate is continental: cold winters with frost risk, hot summers and, crucially, a long, dry and warm autumn. The Bodrog and Tisza, with their oxbows and marshes, create the humid mornings that start botrytis, while the hills shield the slopes from northern winds. Vineyards lie mostly on south, south-east and south-west slopes between about 120 and 300 m. Below ground the region is honeycombed with cellars cut into tuff, some from the 13th to 16th centuries, held at about 10 to 12 °C and high humidity. Their walls are coated with a black, felt-like mould (*Cladosporium cellare* in the specification, now usually classified as *Zasmidium cellare*) that feeds on alcohol and volatile compounds in the air and helps keep humidity at 85 to 95 percent: the slow, cool, moist ageing that defines classic Tokaji.
regions.grapes: Six varieties are permitted for Tokaji. Furmint dominates (roughly two-thirds of plantings): late-budding, late-ripening, thick-skinned at first but prone to botrytis, with searing acidity and a smoky, quince and pear core. Hárslevelű ('linden leaf') adds perfume, honey and spice and is the main partner in Aszú. Sárgamuskotály (Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains) gives grapey lift and occasional single-varietal sweet wines. Kövérszőlő, a near-lost old variety identical to Romania's Grasă de Cotnari, botrytises readily and is being replanted by a few growers. Zéta (Furmint x Bouvier, bred at Tarcal and once called Oremus) ripens early and rots reliably, so it was planted for aszú after the 1950s; Kabar (Hárslevelű x Bouvier, also from Tarcal) is the rarest.
regions.styles:
*Eszencia*: the free-run juice that oozes from aszú berries under their own weight, often 450 to 700 g/l of sugar and occasionally above 900. It ferments for years to 1.2 to 8% alcohol, is sold in tiny bottles and is traditionally taken by the spoonful. Rules: at least 450 g/l sugar; no more than 6 l from 100 kg of aszú berries.

*Aszú*: aszú berries are macerated for one to several days in fermenting must or young wine of the same vintage, pressed and fermented slowly, then aged at least 18 months in wood and released no earlier than 1 January of the third year after harvest. Since the 2013 reform the minimum residual sugar is 120 g/l (the old 5 puttonyos level). The 'puttonyos' figure, historically the number of 20 to 25 kg hods (*puttony*) of aszú paste added to a 136-litre Gönc cask, is now optional; '6 puttonyos' requires at least 150 g/l. The old 3 and 4 puttonyos wines and Aszú-Eszencia (a 7 puttonyos equivalent) are gone as categories.

*Szamorodni* ('as it was born', from Polish): whole bunches with their natural share of botrytis are crushed and fermented together. *Száraz* (dry) Szamorodni must spend at least 24 months in cask, traditionally under a film of yeast in ullaged barrels, which gives a nutty, saline, sherry-like wine. *Édes* (sweet) Szamorodni needs at least 60 g/l under the current specification (45 g/l in the 2013 rules) and six months in wood.

*Fordítás* ('turned over'): must or wine poured over the pressed aszú paste and fermented again. *Máslás* (from 'copy'): wine aged on aszú lees. Both are now rare, rich, and at least 60 g/l.

*Késői szüretelésű* (late harvest): a modern style, mostly unoaked, at least 45 g/l, made from overripe and partly botrytised grapes; the entry point to sweet Tokaj. Dry and off-dry whites (Furmint, Hárslevelű, blends) now make up a large share of production, increasingly as single-vineyard (dűlő) wines, and traditional-method sparkling *pezsgő* must spend at least 15 months in bottle (24 for vintage wines).
regions.classification: The 18th-century class system (first, second, third class vineyards, with a few 'great first growths' such as Mézes Mály and Szarvas above them) survives as tradition, not law. Today's legal framework is the Tokaj PDO specification managed by the Tokaj Wine Region Council of Growers (Tokaji Borvidék Hegyközségi Tanács). Only vineyard land rated Class I or II in the cadastre can produce Tokaji. Single-vineyard names may appear only if the dűlő is listed in the annex (for Mád alone, 27 dűlők from Bacskai to Vilmány), and such wines must be 100% from that site and vintage, 100% of the named variety if one is stated, and cropped at no more than 6 t/ha. A village name may appear under rules set by the local growers' council. Yields are capped at 10 t/ha for the sweet specialities and late harvest, 14 t/ha for dry wines, and aszú berries picked separately count five times their weight toward the limit. Royal Tokaji's labels still cite the historic classification ('Great First Growth' Mézes Mály, 'First Growth' Szent Tamás, Betsek, Nyulászó, Birsalmás), and groups such as the Mád Circle (Mádi Kör) of growers run their own village-wine rules.

regions.name: Balaton
regions.tagline: Basalt buttes, red sandstone and the largest lake in Central Europe: Hungary's white-wine heartland.
regions.summary: The Balaton region wraps around Lake Balaton, 77 km long and shallow, which warms quickly in summer, reflects light onto the north-shore slopes and slows autumn frost. Six wine districts belong to it: Badacsony, Balaton-felvidék (the Balaton Uplands), Balatonfüred-Csopak and Nagy-Somló on or behind the north shore, Balatonboglár on the south shore and Zala to the west. On top of them sit the umbrella PDO Balaton, the single-community PDOs Tihany and Csopak, the Káli basin PDO, Somló's own PDO and, since 2025, Füred. The north shore is the drama: a row of extinct volcanoes, the 'witness hills' (*tanúhegyek*) of Badacsony, Szent György-hegy, Gulács and Csobánc, flat-topped basalt buttes rising from the plain, plus red Permian sandstone around Csopak and limestone in the Káli basin. The wines are whites first: Olaszrizling everywhere, Szürkebarát (Pinot Gris), Furmint, Hárslevelű, Juhfark on Somló, and the rare Kéknyelű on Badacsony.
regions.history: The Romans planted around Balaton, and the Benedictine abbey of Tihany, founded in 1055, owned vineyards from its first charter (a document famous for containing the oldest surviving written Hungarian words). The north-shore hills became the summer seat of the Hungarian gentry in the 18th and 19th centuries; their stone press houses (*présház*) still dot the slopes. Poets followed: Sándor Kisfaludy kept a press house on Badacsony from 1798. Phylloxera devastated the region in the 1880s, and socialist-era state farms flattened its reputation. The revival since 2000 has been driven by small growers who bottle single hills and single varieties.
regions.terroir: Annual temperatures are mild for Hungary and the lake effect extends the season. Basalt and basaltic tuff weather to dark, stony soils that give saline, smoky whites; Permian red sandstone and slate at Csopak give crisp, mineral Olaszrizling; loess and sand on the south shore make lighter, fruitier wines.
regions.grapes: Olaszrizling (Welschriesling) is the regional grape; Szürkebarát (Pinot Gris), Furmint, Hárslevelű, Kéknyelű, Juhfark, Rajnai rizling and Sauvignon Blanc follow. Reds (Kékfrankos, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet) matter mainly at Balatonboglár.
regions.styles: Mostly dry whites, from fresh lakeside Olaszrizling to structured, oak-aged volcanic whites; traditional-method sparkling at Somló and Balatonboglár; rosé and light reds on the south shore.
regions.classification: Each district is a PDO. Csopak (2020) and Füred (2025) are narrower village PDOs with stricter rules; Csopak's growers built a 'Csopak Codex' focused on Olaszrizling and named sites. The Balaton PDO is a regional umbrella over all of them.

regions.name: Upper Hungary
regions.tagline: Volcanic foothills of the Mátra and Bükk, home of Bull's Blood and the cellar-lined valleys of Eger.
regions.summary: Upper Hungary (Felső-Magyarország, also called the Eger wine region) is the band of foothills along the southern edge of the North Hungarian Mountains: the Mátra around Gyöngyös, the Bükk around Eger and Miskolc. It holds three districts: Eger, famous for Egri Bikavér and Egri Csillag; Mátra, Hungary's second-largest hill district, mostly white; and Bükk, small and cool. Debrő, at the eastern foot of the Mátra, has its own PDO for Hárslevelű. The rocks are volcanic: rhyolite tuff, so soft that whole streets of cellars are carved into it, andesite in the Mátra and some limestone. The climate is cooler than the south, so Eger's reds are fresher and more fragrant than Villány's or Szekszárd's.
regions.history: Eger's bishops owned great vineyards from the Middle Ages. István Dobó's defence of Eger castle against the Ottomans in 1552 gave the region its founding legend, although Eger fell in 1596 and stayed Ottoman until 1687. After the reconquest, Serbian and German settlers rebuilt the vineyards, and Kadarka became the base of the red blend later sold as Bikavér. Phylloxera and then state farming flattened quality, and Egri Bikavér became a cheap export label; since the 1990s producers such as Tibor Gál, Thummerer, St. Andrea, Bolyki, Kovács Nimród and Demeter have rebuilt it.
regions.terroir: Rhyolite and andesite tuffs, clay and some limestone on south-facing slopes from about 150 to 400 m. The mountains protect from the north; harvests are later and acidity higher than in the south.
regions.grapes: Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Blauburger for reds; Olaszrizling, Leányka, Királyleányka, Hárslevelű, Furmint, Chardonnay, Muscat Ottonel and Tramini for whites.
regions.styles: Egri Bikavér (red blend) and Egri Csillag (white blend) in a three-step pyramid; varietal Pinot Noir and Kékfrankos; aromatic dry whites in the Mátra; Debrő Hárslevelű.
regions.classification: Eger runs a quality pyramid of Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior for its two blends, with tighter yield limits, longer ageing and mapped vineyards at each step. Mátra, Bükk and Debrői Hárslevelű are separate PDOs.

regions.name: Northern Pannonia
regions.tagline: From the shores of Lake Fertő to the cellars under Budapest: cool, windy, limestone country.
regions.summary: Northern Pannonia (Felső-Pannon, the north-western Transdanubian region) collects five districts strung between the Austrian border and Budapest: Sopron on Lake Fertő (Neusiedlersee), Pannonhalma below the Benedictine archabbey, Mór in the Vértes hills, Neszmély on the Danube bend and Etyek-Buda on the limestone plateau west of the capital. Newer, smaller PDOs include Kőszeg (2025) near the Austrian border and Etyeki pezsgő (2025) for Etyek's sparkling wine. It is the coolest part of Hungary, so whites are crisp and aromatic and the red speciality is Kékfrankos.
regions.history: This is the most Germanic corner of Hungarian wine: Sopron's *poncichter* growers, Mór's Swabian resettlers after the Ottoman wars, the Budafok cellars where József Törley set up his champagne house in 1882. Pannonhalma's monks have tended vines since the abbey's foundation in 996, and Kőszeg has recorded the growth of the vine shoots on St George's Day every year since 1740.
regions.terroir: Limestone, loess and brown forest soils, with schist and gneiss in the Sopron hills. Constant north-westerly winds keep the vines dry and cool.
regions.grapes: Kékfrankos (Sopron), Ezerjó (Mór), Chardonnay, Olaszrizling, Zöld veltelini (Grüner Veltliner), Sauvignon Blanc, Irsai Olivér, Pinot Noir and Zweigelt.
regions.styles: Crisp dry whites, Kékfrankos reds, and Hungary's most important traditional-method sparkling wines from Etyek-Buda.
regions.classification: Five district PDOs plus Kőszeg and Etyeki pezsgő.

regions.name: Pannon
regions.tagline: Hungary's warm south: Villány's Cabernet Franc, Szekszárd's loess and Kadarka, Pécs's Cirfandli.
regions.summary: The Pannon region is the south of Transdanubia, between the Danube and the Drava, at the same latitude as Bordeaux's northern tip but with a warmer, sub-Mediterranean touch. Four districts: Villány, Hungary's red-wine star on the southern flank of the Villány hills; Szekszárd, on deep loess hills above the Danube floodplain; Tolna, a large district of lighter wines; and Pécs, on the southern slopes of the Mecsek. The umbrella PDO Pannon covers them all.
regions.history: Roman Sopianae (Pécs) had vineyards. After the 1687 reconquest from the Ottomans, German settlers ('Swabians') rebuilt Villány and much of Tolna, while Serbs brought Kadarka to Szekszárd. Zsigmond Teleki's rootstock nursery at Villány (from 1881) helped save Hungary from phylloxera. After 1990 Villány's family wineries, many of German origin (Bock, Gere, Tiffán, Polgár), led Hungary's first quality revolution and set up the first Hungarian origin-control scheme.
regions.terroir: Limestone and loess in Villány, deep loess with red clay (*vörösagyag*) in Szekszárd, and varied sediments and some granite in the Mecsek. Long hot summers and mild autumns ripen Bordeaux varieties reliably.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Portugieser (Kékoportó), Kékfrankos and Kadarka; Cirfandli (Zierfandler) in Pécs; Olaszrizling and Chardonnay for whites.
regions.styles: Full-bodied Bordeaux-style reds and Franc in Villány; silkier, spicier Bikavér and Kadarka in Szekszárd; whites and some sparkling in Pécs and Tolna.
regions.classification: Villány's pyramid (Classicus, Prémium and the Villányi Franc category, plus single-vineyard wines) and Szekszárd's Bikavér rules lead; Pécs and Tolna are looser. All are PDOs under the Pannon umbrella.

regions.name: Danube
regions.tagline: The sandy Great Plain between the Danube and the Tisza: where Hungary's vines outran phylloxera.
regions.summary: The Danube region (Duna borrégió) covers the Great Plain (Alföld) between the Danube and the Tisza: three districts, Kunság (the country's largest), Csongrád and Hajós-Baja, joined under the umbrella PDO Duna. Smaller PDOs pick out special corners: Izsáki Arany Sárfehér for the high-acid Sárfehér on the Izsák sands, Monor near Budapest (2018) and Soltvadkerti (2020). Roughly a third or more of Hungary's vineyards are here, mostly on flat sand, producing everyday wine, base wine for sparkling and some good-value whites.
regions.history: Phylloxera cannot survive in loose, shifting sand. When it destroyed the hill vineyards in the 1880s the state promoted planting on the Plain: a demonstration vineyard on land donated by Kecskemét (Miklóstelep, 1883) showed the way, and the sands both fed the market and stabilised the drifting dunes. Swabian villages such as Hajós built entire streets of cellars. Under Communism the Plain became the engine of bulk wine for the Soviet bloc.
regions.terroir: Pure sand and sandy loess, a hot, dry continental summer and harsh winters; frost in hollows is the main risk. Wines are generally light, fruity and early drinking.
regions.grapes: Kadarka (historically), Kékfrankos, Ezerjó, Olaszrizling, Cserszegi fűszeres, Irsai Olivér, Kövidinka, Sárfehér, Bianca and other resistant varieties.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, rosé, light reds and sparkling base wine.
regions.classification: District PDOs plus Duna (umbrella), Izsáki Arany Sárfehér, Monor and Soltvadkerti.

regions.name: Primorska
regions.tagline: Collio's other half, the bora-blasted Vipava valley, the red earth of the Karst and the Istrian coast.
regions.summary: Primorska ('Littoral') is Slovenia's western wine region, about 6,300 ha across four PDO districts: Goriška Brda (about 1,800 ha), Vipavska dolina (about 2,100 ha), Kras (about 560 ha) and Slovenska Istra (about 1,850 ha). Brda is the eastern half of Friuli's Collio, cut off by the 1947 border, a landscape of flysch hills and hilltop villages making Rebula, Friulano (Sauvignonasse, called Zeleni sauvignon or Jakot locally), Malvazija and Merlot. Vipava is a long valley where the bora wind can gust above 150 km/h; its native Zelen and Pinela grow beside Rebula and international varieties. The Karst is a limestone plateau of red earth, dry stone walls and thin soil famous for Teran and Vitovska. Slovenska Istra, around Koper, Izola and Piran, makes Malvazija and Refošk on the warm coast.
regions.history: Brda and Vipava were Habsburg lands with Venetian influence; Brda was split between Italy and Yugoslavia in 1947, and Klet Brda, founded in 1957 at Dobrovo, gathered the Slovenian side's growers into Slovenia's largest cooperative. The region was the centre of the macerated-white revival from the 1990s.
regions.terroir: Flysch (*opoka*), layered marl and sandstone that crumbles into well-drained soil, in Brda, Vipava and Istra; terra rossa over karst limestone on the Kras. Sub-Mediterranean climate; the bora dries the vines and limits disease.
regions.grapes: Rebula, Malvazija, Zeleni sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Sivi pinot, Zelen, Pinela, Vitovska; Refošk/Teran, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Fresh and macerated whites, Teran, Merlot-based reds, sweet Pikolit, traditional-method sparkling (Movia Puro).
regions.classification: Four district PDOs plus the Teran PTP/PDO on the Karst.

regions.name: Podravje
regions.tagline: Steep Styrian terraces and Pannonian plains: crisp aromatic whites, Šipon and the world's oldest vine.
regions.summary: Podravje, the Drava basin in north-east Slovenia, is the largest region and has two PDO districts: Štajerska Slovenija (about 5,400 ha, Slovenian Styria) and Prekmurje (about 440 ha, across the Mura). Štajerska's sub-districts include Maribor, Radgona-Kapela, Ljutomer-Ormož (with the hilltop village of Jeruzalem), Haloze, Slovenske gorice, Šmarje-Virštanj and the Srednje Slovenske gorice. The style is cool-climate whites with piercing acidity: Laški rizling, Šipon, Sauvignon Blanc, Renski rizling, Traminec, Muškat and Kerner, plus sweet late-harvest and ice wines.
regions.history: Roman Poetovio (Ptuj) was a wine town; the Minorites built a cellar there in 1239. Maribor's Old Vine dates to before the mid-17th century. Clotar Bouvier made sparkling wine at Gornja Radgona from 1852. Large socialist-era cellars (Vinag in Maribor, Ptujska klet, Radgonske gorice) still exist.
regions.terroir: Marl, sandstone and clay hills, often terraced on slopes of 30 degrees or more; continental climate with cold winters and warm, dry autumns that allow botrytis and ice wine.
regions.grapes: Laški rizling, Šipon, Sauvignon Blanc, Renski rizling, Sivi pinot, Traminec, Muškat ottonel, Rumeni muškat, Ranina, Kerner, Modra frankinja, Modri pinot.
regions.styles: Dry aromatic whites, late harvest, berry selection and ice wine, traditional-method sparkling.
regions.classification: Two PDO districts; sub-districts appear on labels.

regions.name: Posavje
regions.tagline: The Sava and Krka hills of zidanice cottages, tart Cviček and the sand caves of Bizeljsko.
regions.summary: Posavje, along the Sava and Krka rivers in south-east Slovenia, has three PDO districts: Dolenjska (about 1,350 ha), Bizeljsko Sremič (about 700 ha) and Bela krajina (about 300 ha). It is the country's most traditional wine landscape, with hills covered in small vineyards and weekend cottages (*zidanice*), and its emblem wines are blends rather than varietals: Cviček (light, tart, low-alcohol, made from red and white grapes together), Metliška črnina and Belokranjec in Bela krajina, and Bizeljčan. Fine sweet wines (*ledeno vino*, *jagodni izbor*) and sparkling wines are made in Bizeljsko and Bela krajina too.
regions.history: Monasteries such as Pleterje and Kostanjevica shaped the vineyards in the Middle Ages; a strong smallholder culture survived the socialist period.
regions.terroir: Marl, clay and sandstone hills; Bizeljsko's quartz sands; continental climate.
regions.grapes: Žametovka, Modra frankinja, Kraljevina, Laški rizling, Rumeni plavec, Ranfol, Portugalka, Šentlovrenka, Rumeni muškat.
regions.styles: Light red-white blends (Cviček), red blends (Metliška črnina, Bizeljčan), white blends (Belokranjec), sweet wines and sparkling.
regions.classification: Three district PDOs plus four PTP wines: Cviček, Metliška črnina, Belokranjec and Bizeljčan.

regions.name: Istria and Kvarner
regions.tagline: Heart-shaped Istria, its hill towns and red earth: Malvazija, Teran and Momjan Muscat.
regions.summary: Istria is a peninsula shared with Slovenia and Italy, and its Croatian part is the PDO Hrvatska Istra, about 3,000 to 4,000 ha today against roughly 44,000 ha in the late 19th century before phylloxera. Kvarner, the gulf and islands to the east (Krk, Cres, Rab, Pag), forms the Hrvatsko primorje PDO. Istria's emblem is Malvazija Istarska, made as a fresh, saline white, as a rich oak-aged wine or as a skin-macerated amber wine; the red is Teran, with Refošk, Merlot and Cabernet. The old Venetian hill towns of the interior (Motovun, Grožnjan, Momjan, Buje) look over vineyards of red, white and grey soils, and Momjan's sweet muscat has its own PDO. Producers include Kozlović, Matošević, Roxanich, Clai, Coronica, Trapan, Kabola, Benvenuti, Cattunar and Arman. On Krk, the native Žlahtina is the island's white, centred on Vrbnik.
regions.history: Romans, Venetians and Habsburgs all ruled Istria; under Venice its wine went across the Adriatic. After 1945 the peninsula went to Yugoslavia and many Italian-speaking families left. The 1990s and 2000s brought a revival led by small family wineries and the Istrian Malvazija Festival.
regions.terroir: Terra rossa over limestone on the west coast (warm, red-fruited wines), grey and white flysch marl (*bijela* and *siva zemlja*) in the north and centre (finer, more acid-driven whites), and karst on Kvarner's islands. Mediterranean climate, cooler and windier inland.
regions.grapes: Malvazija Istarska, Teran, Refošk, Muškat momjanski, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon; Žlahtina on Krk.
regions.styles: Dry whites (fresh to macerated), Teran reds, sweet Muscat, some sparkling.
regions.classification: PDOs Hrvatska Istra, Hrvatsko primorje and Muškat momjanski (all within the regional PDO Primorska Hrvatska).

regions.name: Dalmatia
regions.tagline: Karst cliffs, island fields walled by Greeks and the wild-hearted Plavac Mali: the Adriatic's most dramatic vineyards.
regions.summary: Dalmatia stretches 400 km from Zadar to Dubrovnik and includes the islands of Brač, Hvar, Korčula, Vis, Šolta and Lastovo, the Pelješac peninsula and the karst hinterland (Dalmatinska zagora). Three subregional PDOs cover it (Sjeverna Dalmacija, Srednja i Južna Dalmacija, Dalmatinska zagora) plus the site PDOs Dingač and Ponikve on Pelješac. The red is Plavac Mali, at its most extreme on the south face of Pelješac at Dingač and Postup, where 45-degree slopes of crumbling dolomite drop straight into the sea and the vines get direct sun, reflected light from the water and radiated heat from the stones. Babić rules around Primošten and Šibenik, where vines grow in tiny walled pockets on bare limestone. The whites are island natives: Pošip and Grk on Korčula, Bogdanuša on Hvar, Vugava on Vis, Maraština and Debit along the coast, Kujundžuša around Imotski. Prošek, a sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, is the traditional dessert wine.
regions.history: Greek colonists on Vis and Hvar in the 4th century BC planted vines in the Stari Grad Plain. Venice ruled much of the coast from the 15th to 18th centuries, and Dubrovnik (Ragusa) kept its own republic and its own vineyards on Pelješac, defended by the walls of Ston. Phylloxera arrived late, in the 1890s; before that, Dalmatian wine boomed as French vineyards died, and the subsequent collapse drove emigration to California and Chile. Dingač became Croatia's first protected wine in 1961. In 2001 Crljenak Kaštelanski (Zinfandel) was rediscovered at Kaštela. Miljenko 'Mike' Grgić, the Croatian-born winemaker behind Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay that won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, returned to found Grgić Vina at Trstenik on Pelješac in 1996.
regions.terroir: Karst limestone and dolomite, terra rossa in hollows, sand at Lumbarda; very hot, dry summers, high UV, sea reflection and strong winds (bura, jugo, maestral). Dry farming on steep slopes, often with goblet-trained bush vines.
regions.grapes: Plavac Mali, Babić, Tribidrag (Crljenak Kaštelanski), Lasina, Dobričić, Plavina; Pošip, Grk, Bogdanuša, Vugava, Maraština, Debit, Kujundžuša, Cetinka.
regions.styles: Powerful reds, island whites, rosé (*opolo*), and prošek.
regions.classification: Three subregional PDOs plus Dingač and Ponikve; Postup (protected in 1967) survives as a traditional name and vineyard position within Srednja i Južna Dalmacija.

regions.name: Slavonia and Croatian Danube
regions.tagline: The Golden Valley of Graševina, Cistercian cellars and the loess terraces of the Danube at Ilok.
regions.summary: Eastern continental Croatia (PDO Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska) splits into Slavonija (the hills around the Požega basin, Kutjevo, Orahovica, Đakovo and Slavonski Brod) and Hrvatsko Podunavlje (the Croatian Danube: Baranja, Erdut and Ilok on the Srijem ridge). Graševina is king, making everything from fresh, appley whites to oak-aged and botrytised wines; Traminac, Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Frankovka follow. Kutjevo's 'Golden Valley' (Vallis Aurea) is the heart: Kutjevo d.d. (with about 430 ha of its own vines), Krauthaker, Enjingi, Galić, Feravino and others. On the Danube, Iločki podrumi, Erdutski vinogradi and Belje work big estates on loess.
regions.history: Romans planted on the Srijem ridge (the emperor Probus, born at Sirmium, is credited with planting vines on nearby Fruška Gora). Cistercians founded Kutjevo in 1232; after the Ottomans, Jesuits and then noble families (the Turković family at Kutjevo, the Odescalchi at Ilok) rebuilt the estates. The 1990s war hit the Danube vineyards hard.
regions.terroir: Loess, clay and marl on south-facing slopes of the Papuk and Krndija hills; thick loess on the Danube terraces. Continental climate with hot summers and cold winters.
regions.grapes: Graševina, Traminac, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Blanc, Frankovka, Zweigelt, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sweet late-harvest and ice wines, reds from Frankovka and Bordeaux varieties.
regions.classification: PDOs Slavonija and Hrvatsko Podunavlje within Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska.

regions.name: Croatian Uplands
regions.tagline: The hills around Zagreb: sparkling Plešivica, aromatic Međimurje Pušipel and Moslavina's Škrlet.
regions.summary: The Croatian Uplands (PDO Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska) is a ring of hill country around Zagreb divided into five subregions: Plešivica (west of Zagreb, known for traditional-method sparkling and amphora wines), Zagorje-Međimurje (the northern hills, where Pušipel, local Furmint, is the signature), Prigorje-Bilogora, Moslavina (home of the native Škrlet) and Pokuplje along the Kupa. Small family estates dominate: Tomac, Korak, Jagunić and Režek in Plešivica, Bolfan, Štampar and Cmrečnjak in Zagorje-Međimurje.
regions.history: These were Habsburg-Hungarian lands with strong German and Austrian influence; vineyards are small, often weekend plots with cottages (*klijeti*).
regions.terroir: Marl, clay and limestone hills, cooler and wetter than the east.
regions.grapes: Graševina, Pušipel (Furmint), Sauvignon, Rhine Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Škrlet, Kraljevina, Portugizac.
regions.styles: Crisp whites, sparkling wines, Portugizac nouveau, late harvest.
regions.classification: Five subregional PDOs within Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska.

regions.name: Vojvodina
regions.tagline: Fruška Gora's monasteries, Sremski Karlovci's Bermet and the Banat hills of Vršac.
regions.summary: Vojvodina, the autonomous north, is flat Pannonian plain broken by two hill islands that hold its best vineyards. Fruška Gora is a 75 km ridge on the Danube's right bank above Novi Sad, covered with forest, sixteen Orthodox monasteries and vineyards on loess and marl; Sremski Karlovci, at its foot, is the historic wine town and the home of Bermet. In the Banat to the east, the Vršac hills are the only real elevation; Vršac's vineyards once covered about 10,000 ha and its cellar complex, built in 1968, was among the largest in Europe. The sands of Subotica-Horgoš and Deliblato and the lakeside of Palić complete the picture. Riesling, Graševina, Kreaca, Sremska Zelenika, Morava, Tamjanika, Frankovka and Bordeaux varieties dominate.
regions.history: Habsburg rule from 1699 to 1918 brought German, Hungarian and Slovak settlers and Austrian wine culture; Sremski Karlovci was the Serbian Orthodox metropolitan seat and a wine-trading town. The Karlovci Gymnasium and the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz were signed here.
regions.terroir: Loess and marl on Fruška Gora; loess and schist at Vršac; sand dunes in the north and at Deliblato.
regions.grapes: Graševina, Riesling, Sremska Zelenika, Morava, Kreaca, Tamjanika, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Frankovka, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Crisp whites, Bermet, reds from Fruška Gora's warmer slopes.
regions.classification: PGIs Srem, Fruška Gora, Banat, Southern Banat, Northern Banat, Banat-Tisa, Vršac, Bela Crkva, Deliblato Sands, Subotica-Horgoš Sands, Palić, Horgoš and others.

regions.name: Šumadija and Central Serbia
regions.tagline: The rolling heart of Serbia: Oplenac's royal winery, Župa's Prokupac and the Morava valleys.
regions.summary: Central Serbia is hilly, rural and continental. Šumadija ('forest land') around Topola, Aranđelovac and Kragujevac holds the King's Winery at Oplenac and estates such as Aleksandrović; to the south, the West Morava and Rasina valleys lead to Župa around Aleksandrovac, Serbia's self-styled wine capital, warm and sheltered, where Prokupac and Tamjanika thrive. Levač, Jagodina, Kruševac, Trstenik and Belgrade's own hills (Grocka, Kosmaj, Dubona) are other districts.
regions.history: Medieval Serbia's monasteries (Studenica, Žiča, Ljubostinja) held vineyards; Topola was the seat of Karađorđe's First Serbian Uprising (1804) and the Karađorđević dynasty built its mausoleum and winery at Oplenac.
regions.terroir: Clay, loess and limestone hills; continental climate with hot summers.
regions.grapes: Prokupac, Tamjanika, Smederevka, Graševina, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Prokupac and Tamjanika varietals, international reds and whites.
regions.classification: PGIs Šumadija-Velika Morava, Oplenac, Župa, Kruševac, Levač, Jagodina, Trstenik, Grocka, Kosmaj, Belgrade and others.

regions.name: Eastern Serbia
regions.tagline: The Timok and Negotin Krajina: stone cellar villages, Bagrina and black Tamjanika near the Danube.
regions.summary: Eastern Serbia covers the Timok valley and the Negotin Krajina by the Danube's Iron Gates and the Bulgarian and Romanian borders, plus Knjaževac, Zaječar and Bor. Its unique heritage is the *pivnice*: villages of stone cellars at Rajac, Rogljevo and Štubik, built apart from the homes, where families made and stored wine and stayed during the harvest. Bagrina, black Tamjanika and Gamay are local specialities; Matalj, Raj and Rajac Cellars are among the producers.
regions.history: The pivnice date mostly from the 19th century; Negotin wine was exported to France during phylloxera. The Negotin Pivnice were placed on Serbia's UNESCO Tentative List in 2010.
regions.terroir: Sandstone and limestone hills, warm continental climate tempered by the Danube.
regions.grapes: Prokupac, Bagrina, Tamjanika (white and black), Gamay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Riesling.
regions.styles: Reds, aromatic whites.
regions.classification: PGIs Negotin, Krajina, Rajac, Timok, Zaječar, Knjaževac, Bor, Boljevac, Mihajlovac, Ključ and others.

regions.name: Southern Serbia
regions.tagline: Toplica and Niš: Prokupac's homeland in the warm south.
regions.summary: Southern Serbia (Niš, Toplica, Leskovac, Vranje, Pirot) is the historic home of Prokupac, named after the town of Prokuplje in the Toplica valley. Warm summers ripen it to fuller, spicier wines than in the north. Niš's Matejevac hills, Toplica and Vranje are among the most active districts, with wineries such as Aleksić, Kovačević and Doja reviving the grape.
regions.history: Niš (Roman Naissus), birthplace of Constantine the Great, had vineyards in antiquity; Prokuplje gave its name to the grape in the Middle Ages.
regions.terroir: Hills of clay, schist and limestone; warm continental to sub-Mediterranean influence in the south.
regions.grapes: Prokupac, Tamjanika, Smederevka, Vranac, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Prokupac reds and rosé.
regions.classification: PGIs Toplica, Prokuplje, Niš, Nišava, Nišava-Južna Morava, Leskovac, Vranje, Pirot and others.

regions.name: Herzegovina
regions.tagline: The Neretva's hot karst country: Žilavka, Blatina and monks' Vranac.
regions.summary: Herzegovina, the southern part of the country, holds nearly all the vineyards: around Mostar and the Neretva valley, Čitluk (with Međugorje), Ljubuški, Stolac and Čapljina in the west, and Trebinje in the south-east near Dubrovnik. Čitluk is the largest wine municipality and home of Vinarija Čitluk and Podrumi Andrija; Trebinje's Tvrdoš monastery and Vukoje estate make the region's best-known Vranac.
regions.history: Austro-Hungarian rule from 1878 brought viticultural schools and a market in Vienna; under socialism the Hepok cooperative dominated; the 1990s war broke the industry, and family wineries rebuilt it.
regions.terroir: Karst limestone, terra rossa and stony alluvium; summers up to 40 °C; dry and windy.
regions.grapes: Žilavka, Blatina, Trnjak, Vranac, Plavac Mali, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Dry whites and reds, rosé.
regions.classification: Traditional names Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina; no EU-recognised GIs.

regions.name: Lake Skadar Basin
regions.tagline: The Zeta plain, Ćemovsko polje and the terraces of Crmnica: Montenegro's Vranac heartland.
regions.summary: The Montenegrin basin of Lake Skadar is the main wine region, from the Zeta plain and Ćemovsko polje around Podgorica to the terraced slopes of Crmnica above Virpazar and the Riječki subregion around Rijeka Crnojevića. Plantaže's 2,300 ha vineyard dominates, but family wineries in Crmnica (Godinje, Virpazar) keep older traditions and Kratošija vines.
regions.history: Crmnica wine was considered the best in Montenegro in the 19th century and won prizes in London in 1907.
regions.terroir: Karst limestone, gravel and terra rossa; hot Mediterranean summers moderated by the lake.
regions.grapes: Vranac, Kratošija, Krstač, Žižak, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Full reds, Krstač whites, rosé.
regions.classification: Legal region (2017) with seven subregions.

regions.name: Montenegrin Coast
regions.tagline: Boka Kotorska to Ulcinj: small coastal vineyards above the Adriatic.
regions.summary: The coastal region runs from the Bay of Kotor through Budva and Bar to Ulcinj, with small vineyards on the slopes above the sea. Budva's medieval statute contains the first record of Kratošija.
regions.history: Venetian rule kept coastal vineyards alive during the Ottoman period.
regions.terroir: Limestone and flysch slopes; Mediterranean climate.
regions.grapes: Vranac, Kratošija, Krstač, Žižak.
regions.styles: Reds and whites for local consumption.
regions.classification: Legal region (2017) with four subregions.

regions.name: Povardarie
regions.tagline: The Vardar valley and Tikveš: hot, sunny, Vranec-dominated and home to nearly all the wineries.
regions.summary: Povardarie, the Vardar river valley, holds about 85 to 87 percent of the country's vineyards and 90 percent of its wineries. Its subregions include Skopje, Veles, Ovče Pole, Tikveš, Gevgelija-Valandovo and Strumica-Radoviš. Tikveš, around Kavadarci, Negotino and Demir Kapija, is the most famous, with Tikveš winery, Stobi, Bovin, Popova Kula and many smaller estates.
regions.history: Stobi's Roman ruins and Tikveš's 19th-century winery mark the long continuity of wine here.
regions.terroir: Alluvial terraces and clay-loam hills; hot dry summers, cold winters, Aegean influence.
regions.grapes: Vranec, Kratošija, Stanušina, Smederevka, Temjanika, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Ripe, dark reds; fresh whites; bulk wine for export.
regions.classification: Wine region with 8 subregions; first GI 'Vardar Valley' in preparation (2026).

regions.name: Pčinja-Osogovo
regions.tagline: The eastern hills toward Bulgaria: Kratovo, Kočani and Kumanovo.
regions.summary: Pčinja-Osogovo covers the eastern hills along the Pčinja river and the Osogovo mountains toward Bulgaria, with subregions such as Kočani, Kratovo, Kumanovo and Pijanec. It is cooler and higher than the Vardar valley and makes fresher wines.
regions.history: Kratovo sits in the crater of an extinct volcano and has a long winemaking tradition.
regions.terroir: Volcanic and metamorphic soils, continental climate.
regions.grapes: Vranec, Smederevka, Riesling, Kratošija.
regions.styles: Reds and whites.
regions.classification: Wine region with 4 subregions.

regions.name: Pelagonija-Polog
regions.tagline: The high west: Bitola, Prilep, Ohrid and Prespa.
regions.summary: Pelagonija-Polog spans the west, from the Pelagonia plain around Bitola and Prilep to Ohrid and Prespa lakes and Tetovo and Kičevo in the Polog valley. Higher altitudes and lake influence give fresher, lighter wines.
regions.history: Ohrid's monasteries and Bitola's Roman Heraclea Lyncestis recall a long wine history.
regions.terroir: Lake and mountain influence, cooler climate; alluvial and limestone soils.
regions.grapes: Vranec, Smederevka, Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.
regions.styles: Fresher reds and whites.
regions.classification: Wine region with 6 subregions.

regions.name: Northern Albania
regions.tagline: The Zadrima plain and the hills of Shkodër, Lezhë and Mirditë: Kallmet country.
regions.summary: The north (Shkodër, Koplik, Lezhë, Kurbin, Mirditë, Pukë) is the home of Kallmet, grown on the alluvial Zadrima plain and surrounding hills where the Drin reaches the sea. Kantina Arbëri in Mirditë and family wineries around Shkodër and Lezhë lead.
regions.history: The Catholic north kept vineyards through the Ottoman period.
regions.terroir: Alluvial plains and limestone hills; Mediterranean with high rainfall.
regions.grapes: Kallmet, Shesh i Zi, Shesh i Bardhë.
regions.styles: Reds and whites.
regions.classification: UK-protected GIs Shkodër, Koplik, Lezhë, Kurbin, Mirditë, Pukë and others.

regions.name: Central and Southern Albania
regions.tagline: Tirana's Shesh, Berat's Pulës and the Debinë of Korçë and Përmet.
regions.summary: Central and southern Albania include Tirana (Shesh), Durrës and Kavajë on the coast, Berat (Pulës, Çobo winery), Skrapar (Nurellari), Vlorë (Vlosh), and the highlands of Korçë and Përmet (Debinë).
regions.history: Greek and Roman Apollonia, Butrint and Berat give the region a deep wine history.
regions.terroir: Coastal hills, river valleys and continental highlands.
regions.grapes: Shesh i Zi, Shesh i Bardhë, Pulës, Debinë, Vlosh, Serinë, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Reds and whites.
regions.classification: UK-protected GIs Tiranë, Berat, Korçë, Përmet, Vlorë, Skrapar and others.

regions.name: Dukagjin
regions.tagline: Rahovec, Suharekë and Prizren: the sunny south-western hills where nearly all of Kosovo's vines grow.
regions.summary: The Dukagjin plain and its rim of hills in south-western Kosovo contain almost the whole vineyard: Rahovec (about 2,465 ha), Suharekë (575 ha), Prizren (198 ha), Gjakovë (77 ha) and Malishevë (65 ha), as reported by the ministry for 2024. Rahovec town is the wine capital, home of Stone Castle and dozens of family cellars.
regions.history: Yugoslav-era Rahovec exported red wine to West Germany; war and the loss of that market shattered the industry, which has been rebuilding since 2000.
regions.terroir: Hillsides at 300 to 600 m with loamy and red soils; continental climate with Mediterranean air from the Drin valley.
regions.grapes: Vranac, Prokupac, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Smederevka, Riesling, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Mostly reds, some whites and rosé.
regions.classification: No GIs; statistics and licensing by region.

regions.name: Moldavian Hills
regions.tagline: Romania's largest wine region, from noble-rot Cotnari to the vast Vrancea vineyards.
regions.summary: The Moldavian Hills (Dealurile Moldovei) cover eastern Romania between the Carpathians and the Prut, roughly a third of the country's vineyard. In the north, around Iași, lie Cotnari, Iași, Bohotin, Huși and Iana; in the south the huge Vrancea block of Panciu, Odobești and Cotești, one of the largest continuous vineyards in Europe, and Nicorești and Dealu Bujorului in Galați county. Whites dominate: Fetească Albă and Regală, Grasă, Tămâioasă, Frâncușă, Șarba and Galbenă de Odobești, with Băbească Neagră and Fetească Neagră as the reds.
regions.history: The medieval princes of Moldavia, Stephen the Great above all, made Cotnari's wine a court drink; monasteries owned large estates. Under Communism Vrancea and Huși became bulk wine centres, and Huși was linked to Nicolae Ceaușescu's favourite wines.
regions.terroir: Loess, clay and sandstone hills, continental climate with cold winters; Cotnari's autumn fogs favour botrytis.
regions.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Grasă de Cotnari, Tămâioasă Românească, Frâncușă, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Șarba, Zghihară de Huși, Galbenă de Odobești, Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră.
regions.styles: Sweet and semi-sweet aromatic whites, crisp dry whites, sparkling (Panciu), light reds.

regions.name: Muntenia and Oltenia Hills
regions.tagline: The southern Carpathian foothills: Dealu Mare's Fetească Neagră and Drăgășani's crisp whites.
regions.summary: The southern face of the Carpathians, from Buzău and Prahova in the east to Mehedinți in the west, is Romania's red-wine heartland. Dealu Mare ('big hill') is the leading DOC, a 65 km south-facing ridge with Urlați, Valea Călugărească, Ceptura and Merei; Pietroasa at its eastern end is famed for sweet Tămâioasă. West of the Olt, Oltenia has Drăgășani (Crâmpoșie, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac), Sâmburești, Ștefănești, Banu Mărăcine near Craiova, Segarcea (once the royal crown estate) and Mehedinți near the Iron Gates.
regions.history: Dealu Mare was the scene of phylloxera's first Romanian outbreak at Chitorani. Valea Călugărească ('valley of the monks') hosted the national research institute. Segarcea was a royal domain from 1884 to 1948. Prince Știrbey's family estate at Drăgășani was restituted in 2001 and revived.
regions.terroir: South-facing slopes on clay, loess and marls; warm summers and good autumn sunshine ripen red grapes reliably.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac, Tămâioasă Românească, Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Fetească Regală, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Full-bodied reds, aromatic sweet wines (Pietroasa), crisp whites (Drăgășani).
regions.classification: DOCs Dealu Mare, Pietroasa, Drăgășani, Sâmburești, Ștefănești, Banu Mărăcine, Segarcea, Mehedinți; IG Dealurile Munteniei, Dealurile Olteniei.

regions.name: Transylvanian Plateau
regions.tagline: Saxon villages, fortified churches and cool, crisp whites inside the Carpathian arc.
regions.summary: Inside the Carpathian arc, the Transylvanian Plateau sits at 300 to 500 m with a cool continental climate. Its DOCs are Târnave (the valleys of the Târnava Mare and Mică, home of Jidvei, Romania's largest single estate), Alba Iulia, Aiud, Sebeș-Apold and Lechința. The wines are aromatic, high-acid whites: Fetească Regală (discovered at Daneș near Sighișoara), Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris, and traditional-method sparkling.
regions.history: Transylvanian Saxons, German settlers invited by Hungarian kings from the 12th century, built fortified churches in wine villages such as Biertan, Apold and Mediaș; their cellars and vineyards were abandoned after their emigration in 1990, and revival has been slow but real.
regions.terroir: Marl and clay hills, cooler and wetter than the rest of Romania, with a late harvest and high acidity.
regions.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer Roz, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Neuburger, Iordana.
regions.styles: Crisp dry and off-dry whites, sparkling, some Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: DOCs Târnave, Alba Iulia, Aiud, Sebeș-Apold, Lechința; IG Dealurile Transilvaniei.

regions.name: Dobrogea
regions.tagline: Between the Danube and the Black Sea: Romania's sunniest, driest vineyards.
regions.summary: Dobrogea, the land between the lower Danube and the Black Sea, is Romania's sunniest region, with more than 300 sunny days in places and very low rainfall. Murfatlar, near Constanța, is its most famous DOC, known for rich, often sweet, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Muscat Ottonel as well as Fetească Neagră reds. Other DOCs are Oltina and Adamclisi in the south-west, and Babadag and Sarica Niculițel in the north, around the old Hercynian Măcin hills near the Danube Delta.
regions.history: Greek colonies (Histria, Tomis, Callatis) traded wine; the Romans fought for this frontier, leaving Tropaeum Traiani at Adamclisi. Niculițel has a 4th-century Christian martyrs' basilica. Murfatlar's research station and large state winery made it a household name.
regions.terroir: Limestone and loess plateaus, chalky soils at Murfatlar, very warm dry summers; the Black Sea moderates winter.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Muscat Ottonel, Tămâioasă Românească, Columna.
regions.styles: Ripe reds, rich whites, sweet late-harvest wines.
regions.classification: DOCs Murfatlar, Oltina, Adamclisi, Babadag, Sarica Niculițel; IG Dealurile Dobrogei.

regions.name: Banat
regions.tagline: The south-west: Recaș's big modern winery and Serbian-influenced vineyards on the Danube.
regions.summary: The Banat region in south-western Romania borders Serbia and Hungary. Its DOCs are Recaș, built around one of Romania's largest and most modern wineries, and Banat, covering the Moldova Nouă and Dealurile Tirolului areas near the Danube. Cadarcă (Kadarka), Burgund Mare (Blaufränkisch) and Riesling are traditional here; international varieties now dominate.
regions.history: Banat was Habsburg land after 1718, settled by Swabians, Serbs, Romanians and Czechs; Recaș's vineyards date from the 15th century, and the modern winery was rebuilt after 1998 by Romanian and British partners.
regions.terroir: Clay and sandy loams, warm with a sub-Mediterranean touch.
regions.grapes: Cadarcă, Burgund Mare, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Modern varietal reds and whites, sparkling.
regions.classification: DOCs Recaș and Banat; IG Viile Timișului.

regions.name: Crișana and Maramureș
regions.tagline: The western hills toward Hungary: Miniș's Cadarcă and Crișana's white wines.
regions.summary: The western hills of Crișana and Maramureș face the Pannonian plain. Miniș, in the Zărand hills near Arad, is known for Cadarcă red and the local white Mustoasă de Măderat; Crișana, around Oradea and Zalău, makes mostly whites.
regions.history: Miniș is one of the oldest documented vineyard areas in Romania; the region shares Hungarian and Habsburg history with the Carpathian Basin.
regions.terroir: Volcanic and marl slopes in the Zărand hills, clays and sands in Crișana.

regions.name: Danube Terraces and Southern Sands
regions.tagline: The Danube floodplain terraces and sand dunes of the south.
regions.summary: The Danube Terraces and the sandy plains of southern Romania (Sadova-Corabia, Calafat, Dăbuleni) are mostly bulk-wine areas covered by IGs such as Dealurile Olteniei and Terasele Dunării. Însurăței, in Brăila county on the Danube's left bank, gained DOC status in 2018 and produces crisp whites and reds from Fetească Neagră, Syrah and Cabernet.
regions.history: Sandy soils resistant to phylloxera made these plains important for ungrafted vineyards in the 20th century.
regions.terroir: Sand dunes and Danube terraces; hot, dry summers.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian.

regions.name: Danubian Plain
regions.tagline: North Bulgaria between the Danube and the Balkan range: Gamza, Cabernet and the old export wineries.
regions.summary: The Danubian Plain (North Bulgaria) stretches from Vidin in the north-west to Ruse in the east, between the Danube and the Balkan range. It is temperate continental, with hot summers and cold winters, and it produced much of the Cabernet Sauvignon that flooded British shelves in the 1980s from wineries at Suhindol, Svishtov, Pavlikeni and Lyaskovets. Gamza (Kadarka) is the local red, especially around Vidin and Novo Selo, and Pleven's institute bred Rubin. Modern estates include Bononia, Magura, Borovitza, Chateau de Val, Burgozone and Tipchenitza. The PGI Danube Plain (Дунавска равнина) covers the region.
regions.history: Suhindol's cooperative, founded in 1909, is often called the first wine cooperative in Bulgaria; the state wineries of the region supplied the Vinimpex export machine.
regions.terroir: Chernozem and loess plains, limestone and sandstone in the north-west near Belogradchik; Danube influence moderates temperature.
regions.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Rubin, Muscat Ottonel, Chardonnay, Aligoté.
regions.styles: Medium-bodied reds, fresh whites, traditional-method sparkling at Magura.
regions.classification: 13 PDOs plus the Danube Plain PGI.

regions.name: Black Sea
regions.tagline: The north-east and the coast: Dimyat, Riesling and crisp whites near Varna and Pomorie.
regions.summary: The Black Sea region (East Bulgaria) covers the coast from Dobrich to Burgas and the plateau inland around Shumen, Veliki Preslav and Targovishte. The sea moderates the climate and the long autumns suit white grapes: Dimyat, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. The Khan Krum and Preslav cellars are historic white-wine houses; Pomorie, on the southern coast, is known for Dimyat and for brandy.
regions.history: The plateau around Pliska and Preslav was the heart of the First Bulgarian Empire, and Veliki Preslav was its 10th-century capital. Euxinograd, the former royal summer palace near Varna, has kept vineyards on its estate.
regions.terroir: Loess and chernozem on the Dobrudzha plateau, limestone near Shumen, sands near the coast.
regions.grapes: Dimyat, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Ugni Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Fresh and aromatic whites, some reds, brandy.
regions.classification: 12 PDOs including the broad Chernomorski Rayon and Yuzhno Chernomorie.

regions.name: Rose Valley
regions.tagline: The Sub-Balkan valley of roses beneath the Balkan range: Red Misket and cool whites.
regions.summary: The Sub-Balkan region (Подбалкански район) is the long valley between the Balkan range and the Sredna Gora, famous for the Kazanlak rose-oil fields. Its vineyards around Karlovo, Sliven, Sungurlare, Karnobat and Shivachevo make Red Misket (Misket Cherven), Muscat and Riesling whites and some reds. Sungurlare's valley is the classic home of Red Misket.
regions.history: The Valley of the Thracian Kings around Kazanlak holds dozens of Thracian tombs, including the UNESCO-listed Kazanlak tomb (4th century BC).
regions.terroir: Alluvial and cinnamon forest soils in a sheltered valley; cooler than Thrace.
regions.grapes: Misket Cherven, Muscat Ottonel, Riesling, Rkatsiteli, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

regions.name: Thracian Lowlands
regions.tagline: The Maritsa basin and Sakar hills: Mavrud, Rubin and Bulgaria's richest reds.
regions.summary: The Thracian Lowlands (South Bulgaria) follow the Maritsa river from Pazardzhik through Plovdiv, Stara Zagora and Haskovo to the Turkish and Greek borders, closed off by the Rhodopes to the south. It is the warmest large region and the heart of Bulgarian red wine. Mavrud comes from Asenovgrad and Perushtitsa; Rubin, Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah thrive. The Sakar hills near the Turkish border (Lyubimets, Svilengrad, Harmanli) have become a magnet for modern estates such as Katarzyna, Terra Tangra and Castra Rubra. Bessa Valley near Pazardzhik, Zagreus at Vinitsa, Rumelia and Midalidare are other names to know. The PGI Thracian Lowlands (Тракийска низина) covers the region.
regions.history: Thracian sanctuaries, Philippopolis (Plovdiv) and the Roman road across Thrace made this a wine route since antiquity; Mavrud's legend is set here.
regions.terroir: Cinnamon forest soils, smolnitsa black clays and alluvium; hot, dry summers with Mediterranean influence up the Maritsa valley.
regions.grapes: Mavrud, Rubin, Pamid, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Viognier.
regions.styles: Full-bodied reds, rosé, some whites.
regions.classification: 16 PDOs plus the Thracian Lowlands PGI.

regions.name: Struma Valley
regions.tagline: The warm south-west by Greece: Broadleaf Melnik, sandstone pyramids and Bulgaria's smallest town.
regions.summary: The Struma valley (South-West Bulgaria) follows the Struma river south from Blagoevgrad to the Greek border, between the Pirin and Belasitsa mountains. Mediterranean air funnels up the valley, making it Bulgaria's warmest wine area. Its heart is Melnik, a town of about 400 people amid sandstone and conglomerate 'earth pyramids', and its grape is Shiroka Melnishka Loza with its early-ripening offspring Melnik 55. Estates include Villa Melnik, Logodaj, Orbelus, Zlaten Rozhen, Damianitza and Sintica.
regions.history: Melnik's wine was traded to Venice, Austria and England from the 17th and 18th centuries; the town once held about 20,000 people, but most of its Greek population left after 1913. The Kordopulov House cellar of 1754 is its great monument.
regions.terroir: Sandy and sandstone soils, conglomerates and alluvium; hot, dry, sub-Mediterranean.
regions.grapes: Shiroka Melnishka Loza, Ranna Melnishka Loza (Melnik 55), Keratsuda, Sandanski Misket, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah.
regions.styles: Spicy, oak-aged reds; rare whites from Keratsuda and Sandanski Misket.
regions.classification: 4 PDOs.
