appellations.name: Plovdiv
appellations.grapes: Mavrud, Rubin, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pamid
appellations.summary: Plovdiv, the ancient Philippopolis, is the centre of the Thracian Lowlands; its PDO takes in eight municipalities around the city (Asenovgrad, Kuklen, Perushtitsa, Rodopi, Saedinenie, Brezovo, Parvomai). Mavrud, Rubin, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot dominate, and the Brestovitsa area is known for Rubin.

appellations.name: Pazardzhik
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Petit Verdot, Mavrud
appellations.summary: The Pazardzhik PDO lies in the upper Maritsa valley west of Plovdiv (registered with the Septemvri municipality). The area's best-known modern estate is Bessa Valley, founded in 2001 by Count Stephan von Neipperg of Château Canon-la-Gaffelière and Karl-Heinz Hauptmann, which makes Merlot-led reds.

appellations.name: Septemvri
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pamid
appellations.summary: Septemvri, at the western end of the Thracian plain where the Maritsa leaves the mountains, has a PDO for its municipality, mainly for reds from Cabernet, Merlot and Pamid. It sits close to the cooler air descending from the Rila and Rhodope mountains, so the wines are fresher than those of the eastern plain.

appellations.name: Stara Zagora
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Rubin, Syrah
appellations.summary: The Stara Zagora PDO covers the warm southern slopes of the Sredna Gora around the city of Stara Zagora (Bratya Daskalovi and Opan municipalities). It is red-wine country: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Rubin and Syrah.

appellations.name: Oryahovitsa
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Rubin, Mavrud, Syrah
appellations.summary: Oryahovitsa, a village near Stara Zagora on the southern slopes of the Sredna Gora, is home to the Oriachovitza winery, founded in 1936, which became famous in the 1980s for Cabernet-Merlot blends exported to the UK. Its own vineyards sit at 170 to 260 m.

appellations.name: Nova Zagora
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Mavrud, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Nova Zagora covers six municipalities east of Stara Zagora, including Chirpan and Sliven's southern edge, and is the only Bulgarian PDO registered for quality sparkling wine as well as still wine. Edoardo Miroglio's estate at Elenovo and Midalidare near Chirpan are the leading producers.

appellations.name: Sakar
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Mavrud, Cabernet Franc
appellations.summary: Sakar is a low mountain on the Turkish border near Svilengrad, a historic vineyard area that has become one of Bulgaria's most dynamic since 2000. Its warm, dry slopes on granite and sandy soils grow Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah and Mavrud. Katarzyna and Terra Tangra are the best-known estates.

appellations.name: Lyubimets
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Mavrud
appellations.summary: Lyubimets covers the eastern Sakar hills and the lower Maritsa (Harmanli, Lyubimets, Stambolovo, Svilengrad and Topolovgrad municipalities). It is warm Merlot and Cabernet country, and the former state cellar at Lyubimets was a major exporter.

appellations.name: Haskovo
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Mavrud, Rubin
appellations.summary: The Haskovo PDO spans six municipalities in the south-east, from the Rhodope foothills to the Sakar hills. Castra Rubra, named after a nearby Roman fort, is the region's flagship estate.

appellations.name: Stambolovo
appellations.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Stambolovo, a village in the eastern Rhodope foothills near Haskovo, has a PDO for its municipality; its old cellar was known in the export era for Merlot. The hot, dry eastern Rhodope foothills ripen Merlot fully, and Stambolovo Merlot was a familiar export label in the 1980s.

appellations.name: Ivaylovgrad
appellations.grapes: Mavrud, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Ivaylovgrad is in the far south-east near the Greek border, in the warm eastern Rhodopes, close to the Roman villa of Armira with its mosaics. Its PDO is for reds, especially Mavrud and Merlot.

appellations.name: Yambol
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pamid, Rkatsiteli, Muscat Ottonel
appellations.summary: The Yambol PDO covers the Tundzha valley around Yambol and Elhovo (five municipalities). It is a large, warm, flat area of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and whites, once a major exporter.

appellations.name: Bolyarovo
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Bolyarovo, near the Turkish border south-east of Yambol, was registered in 2009 as the last of Bulgaria's PDOs. Its municipality is a remote, hot strip of vineyard on the eastern Sakar plateau.

appellations.name: Karlovo
appellations.grapes: Misket Cherven, Muscat Ottonel, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Karlovo, at the western end of the Rose Valley beneath the Balkan range, covers five municipalities. The area is known for Misket and Red Misket whites. Karlovo is also where the Rose Valley's oil-rose harvest begins each May, and the valley's sheltered position between two mountain ranges keeps its whites aromatic and fresh.

appellations.name: Hisarya
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Rubin, Misket
appellations.summary: Hisarya is a Roman spa town with intact 4th-century walls. Its municipality includes Starosel, where the Thracian temple complex of Chetinyova Mogila stands near a modern winery and spa built around the wine-and-Thracians theme.

appellations.name: Sungurlare
appellations.grapes: Misket Cherven, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer
appellations.summary: Sungurlare's valley, in the eastern Balkan foothills, is the classic home of Misket Cherven (Red Misket), a pink-skinned aromatic white that gives delicate, floral, slightly spicy wines. The PDO covers Sungurlare, Karnobat and Kotel municipalities.

appellations.name: Slavyantsi
appellations.grapes: Misket Cherven, Muscat Ottonel, Riesling
appellations.summary: Slavyantsi, a village in the Sungurlare valley, has its own small PDO, also centred on Red Misket and aromatic whites. Its vineyards share the valley's sheltered, cool-night conditions, which preserve the perfume of Misket. Few producers use the name today; most label their wine Sungurlare or Thracian Lowlands PGI.

appellations.name: Karnobat
appellations.grapes: Misket Cherven, Muscat Ottonel, Rkatsiteli, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Karnobat, inland from Burgas, covers the Karnobat and Straldzha municipalities. It makes whites and reds, and is historically a big brandy and wine centre. Its position between the Black Sea and the eastern Balkan range gives a mild climate suited to both aromatic whites and Bordeaux reds.

appellations.name: Sliven
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pamid, Misket, Rkatsiteli
appellations.summary: Sliven, below the Blue Rocks of the eastern Balkan range, covers four municipalities. Its large winery, Vini Sliven, was a key exporter, and the area grows both reds and whites.

appellations.name: Shivachevo
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pamid
appellations.summary: Shivachevo, a small town in the Tvarditsa municipality at the foot of the Balkan range, has a small PDO for reds and whites from sheltered slopes. The Balkan range protects the vineyards from northern winds, and the area's old cooperative supplied reds for the export trade.

appellations.name: Pomorie
appellations.grapes: Dimyat, Muscat Ottonel, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Pomorie, on a peninsula on the southern Black Sea coast near Burgas, covers four municipalities and is known for Dimyat whites and for grape brandy. The sea moderates temperatures and lengthens the season.

appellations.name: Yuzhno Chernomorie
appellations.grapes: Dimyat, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Yuzhno Chernomorie ('Southern Black Sea Coast') is a broad PDO covering 13 municipalities around Burgas, from Nesebar and Pomorie to Sozopol and Tsarevo. It is used for whites and reds from coastal and inland vineyards.

appellations.name: Chernomorski Rayon
appellations.grapes: Dimyat, Riesling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Traminer, Muscat Ottonel
appellations.summary: Chernomorski Rayon ('Black Sea Region') is the broadest Bulgarian PDO, covering 47 municipalities of north-east Bulgaria from Dobrich and Varna to Shumen, Razgrad and Silistra. It is the umbrella for the region's whites.

appellations.name: Varna
appellations.grapes: Dimyat, Riesling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Varna's PDO covers the vineyards around Bulgaria's main port (Varna, Aksakovo and Byala municipalities). Coastal whites dominate, from Dimyat, Riesling and Chardonnay. The sea keeps autumns long and mild, so whites ripen slowly and keep their acidity.

appellations.name: Evksinograd
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Dimyat
appellations.summary: Evksinograd (Euxinograd) is the former royal summer palace on the coast just north of Varna, built in the 1880s for Prince Alexander of Battenberg. Its estate vineyards give their name to a tiny PDO.

appellations.name: Shumen
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Traminer, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel, Aligoté
appellations.summary: Shumen, on the plateau of north-east Bulgaria near the medieval capitals Pliska and Preslav, covers Shumen, Novi Pazar and Veliki Preslav municipalities. It is known for whites, especially Chardonnay, Traminer and Riesling, from the large Shumen winery.

appellations.name: Veliki Preslav
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Traminer, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Veliki Preslav was the capital of the First Bulgarian Empire in the 10th century. Its PDO covers three municipalities, and its old cellar was famous for Chardonnay and Traminer whites.

appellations.name: Han Krum
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Traminer, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Han Krum, a village named after the 9th-century khan of the Mavrud legend, has a large winery long known for white wines, especially Chardonnay and Traminer. Its PDO covers three municipalities around Shumen and Preslav.

appellations.name: Novi Pazar
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel
appellations.summary: Novi Pazar, east of Shumen on the north-eastern plateau, has a small PDO for whites (registered with the Veliki Preslav municipality). It shares the limestone-rich plateau and cool, breezy conditions that made the Shumen-Preslav area Bulgaria's white-wine heartland under socialism.

appellations.name: Dragoevo
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Aligoté
appellations.summary: Dragoevo, a village near Veliki Preslav, has a small white-wine PDO in the Novi Pazar and Veliki Preslav municipalities. Its vineyards lie on the same limestone plateau as Preslav's, below the 10th-century capital's ruins. Today the name is rarely seen on labels.

appellations.name: Targovishte
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Muscat Ottonel
appellations.summary: Targovishte, in the eastern Danubian plateau, covers the Targovishte and Loznitsa municipalities; its winery is known for Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling. The plateau's cool nights and limestone-rich soils favour crisp whites, as across the north-east.

appellations.name: Varbitsa
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Varbitsa, in the Shumen province at the northern foot of the eastern Balkan range, has a small single-municipality PDO for whites and reds. The village sits in a sheltered valley where the eastern Balkan range meets the north-eastern plateau, so it combines Black Sea freshness with continental warmth.

appellations.name: Suhindol
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Suhindol, in the hills of the central Danubian plain, is a historic wine village whose cooperative, founded in 1909, is often called Bulgaria's first. In the 1980s its Cabernet Sauvignon and Gamza were among the bestselling Bulgarian wines in Britain. The PDO covers Suhindol and Pavlikeni.
appellations.nerd_note: Suhindol's cooperative was founded as 'Gamza' in 1909, named after the local grape, decades before the state took over the industry.

appellations.name: Svishtov
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Gamza, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Svishtov, on the Danube at Bulgaria's northernmost point, covers the Svishtov and Belene municipalities. Its winery was one of the main suppliers of Cabernet Sauvignon for the export boom, from vineyards on loess bluffs above the river.

appellations.name: Pavlikeni
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Gamza
appellations.summary: Pavlikeni, in the central north, has a single-municipality PDO. Its winery was another of the export-era Cabernet and Merlot producers. Its loess-covered hills between the Danube and the Balkan range give medium-bodied, fruity reds, and Gamza also grows here.

appellations.name: Lyaskovets
appellations.grapes: Aligoté, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Lyaskovets, near Veliko Tarnovo, has a long winemaking tradition and a winery known for sparkling and still wines; the PDO covers its municipality. Lyaskovets is a few kilometres from Veliko Tarnovo, capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire, and its winery has a long tradition of traditional-method sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Pleven
appellations.grapes: Rubin, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Gamza
appellations.summary: Pleven is home to Bulgaria's Institute of Viticulture and Enology, where Rubin was bred in 1944, and a wine museum in a cave in Kaylaka park. Its PDO covers four municipalities.

appellations.name: Lovech
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Gamza
appellations.summary: Lovech, at the foot of the central Balkan range, has a small single-municipality PDO for reds and whites from cooler, hillier ground. The town sits on the Osam river where the plain meets the Balkan foothills, so its vineyards are a little cooler and later-ripening than those of the Danube lowlands.

appellations.name: Ruse
appellations.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Traminer, Muscat Ottonel, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Ruse, on the Danube opposite Giurgiu in Romania, covers six municipalities. It is known for whites (Riesling, Chardonnay, Traminer) and some reds; the city was the 19th-century gateway for Western wine culture.

appellations.name: Vratsa
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Vratsa covers seven municipalities of the north-west, from the Balkan foothills to the Danube at Oryahovo and Kozloduy. Burgozone (Oryahovo) and Tipchenitza (Mezdra) are leading estates. The stretch along the Danube is hot and dry, while the Iskar gorge near Mezdra is cooler, so the PDO covers quite different conditions.

appellations.name: Montana
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Montana covers nine municipalities in the north-west between the Balkan range and the Danube; Gamza and Cabernet are the main reds. The area's limestone and loess soils and continental climate give medium-bodied reds, and Gamza here is light and peppery.

appellations.name: Lom
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
appellations.summary: Lom, a Danube port in the north-west, has a single-municipality PDO for reds and whites from loess terraces above the river. Lom was one of Bulgaria's main Danube ports, and its river terraces are warm and well drained.

appellations.name: Vidin
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: Vidin, in Bulgaria's north-west corner, covers Vidin, Novo Selo and Belogradchik municipalities. It is Gamza country, and its estates include Bononia (named after Roman Vidin) and Magura, whose traditional-method sparkling wine ages in a cave decorated with prehistoric paintings near Rabisha.

appellations.name: Novo Selo
appellations.grapes: Gamza, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Novo Selo, a Danube village in the Vidin province, is the classic home of Gamza (Kadarka), which makes light, peppery, red-fruited wines here; the PDO covers its municipality. The Danube moderates temperatures, letting the late-ripening, thin-skinned grape reach full ripeness without losing its freshness.

appellations.name: Lozitsa
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Gamza
appellations.summary: Lozitsa, whose name means 'little vine', is a village in the Nikopol municipality on the Danube. It has a small PDO for wines from the loess bluffs. Nikopol was an important Danube fortress town, and the north-facing river terraces give fresh, medium-bodied wines.

sites.name: Tarcal
sites.text: Tarcal sits on the south-western foot of Tokaj hill, where loess drapes the volcanic core. It holds some of the region's most storied sites (Mézes Mály, Szarvas, Lónyai, Váti, Kassai), the Tokaj viticulture research station where Zéta and Kabar were bred, the Andrássy manor and Királyudvar's winery in a former royal court. Kikelet's loess Furmints showed how perfumed wines from this side of the hill can be.

sites.name: Tokaj
sites.text: The town that gave the region its name sits at the point of Tokaj hill (Kopasz-hegy, 514 m) where the Bodrog flows into the Tisza. River traffic once carried barrels north to Poland. The Rákóczi cellar under the main square, the Tokaj Museum and wineries such as Dobogó and Hétszőlő keep the town at the centre of the trade, and its southern slopes carry Hétszőlő and Szarvas.

sites.name: Mád
sites.text: Mád has the densest concentration of historic first-class vineyards in Tokaj: Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Király, Nyulászó, Birsalmás, Percze and Danczka all surround the village, on rhyolite, andesite and quartzite. Royal Tokaji, Szepsy, Barta and Holdvölgy are based here, and the restored baroque synagogue recalls the Jewish merchants who ran much of the Tokaji trade until 1944.

sites.name: Tállya
sites.text: Tállya, a large market village on the western side of the hills, sits among andesite and rhyolite slopes with dűlők such as Hasznos and Dorgó. Its vineyards were among the Rákóczi family's holdings, and Lajos Kossuth, born in nearby Monok in 1802, was baptised in its Lutheran church. Its wines tend to be firm and spicy.

sites.name: Bodrogkeresztúr
sites.text: Bodrogkeresztúr lies on the Bodrog under the eastern face of Tokaj hill. The Lapis vineyard above it, a terraced rhyolite slope, is the source of Királyudvar's best wines, and the village has given its name to several fine Szamorodni. It is also a Hasidic pilgrimage site, home of the grave of the 'Kerestirer Rebbe', Reb Shayele Steiner.

sites.name: Erdőbénye
sites.text: A forested village in a side valley at the northern edge of the Tokaj hills, Erdőbénye was the region's cooperage centre, making the 136-litre Gönc casks and smaller barrels from local Zemplén oak. Máté Szepsi Laczkó served as pastor here; his memorial house stands on the main street. Béres and others work its cool, high dűlők such as Lőcse, Omlás and Határi.

sites.name: Olaszliszka
sites.text: Olaszliszka, on the Bodrog, carries in its name the 'olasz' (Latin, Italian) settlers invited after the Mongol invasion. Szepsi Laczkó Máté taught here before becoming a pastor. The Frenchman Samuel Tinon chose it for his winery, famous for long flor-aged dry Szamorodni, and Attila Homonna's work on the Határi slope helped put the village's cooler sites on the map.

sites.name: Sárospatak
sites.text: Sárospatak, on the Bodrog in the north-east, was the seat of the Rákóczi princes. Their castle, the Reformed College founded in 1531 (where Comenius taught), and the Rákóczi cellar beneath the town anchor its history. Today it hosts the Pajzos-Megyer winery, and the Megyer hill above Végardó is one of the north's historic vineyards.

sites.name: Sátoraljaújhely
sites.text: The northernmost Tokaj town sits on the Slovak border, facing Slovenské Nové Mesto, which belonged to it until 1920. On its castle hill lies the Oremus vineyard, source of the legendary 1631 aszú attributed to Szepsi Laczkó Máté and the name that the Vega Sicilia-owned estate took for its brand.

sites.name: Mezőzombor
sites.text: Mezőzombor, between Mád and Szerencs, is best known as home to Disznókő, the AXA-owned estate whose single block of about 150 ha takes in the Kapi and Dorgó sites. The village's lower, warmer slopes catch botrytis readily, which made it a reliable source of aszú berries.

sites.name: Rátka
sites.text: Rátka is a small village west of Mád, resettled by German-speaking Catholic families in the 18th century. Its main slope is the Padi-hegy, an andesite hill whose vineyards make firm, smoky Furmint.

sites.name: Szegi
sites.text: Szegi is a small Bodrog-side village between Bodrogkisfalud and Szegilong, with south-facing slopes such as Poklos. Its location on the river makes it a botrytis-friendly spot, and it has drawn several small modern growers.

sites.name: Szegilong
sites.text: Szegilong, on the right bank of the Bodrog north of Szegi, is one of the 27 settlements of the Tokaj PDO and one of the smallest. Its vineyards share the river mists that make the Bodrog side so reliable for noble rot.

sites.name: Bodrogkisfalud
sites.text: Bodrogkisfalud is a riverside village under Tokaj hill's north-eastern flank. The Patricius estate restored an 18th-century manor here, and the Csirke-mál slope above the village is a well-known site.

sites.name: Hercegkút
sites.text: Hercegkút ('Prince's Well') was settled by German Catholic families in the 18th century. Its two cellar rows, Kőporos and Gombos-hegy, with dozens of stone-fronted cellars dug into the hillside, are part of the core zone of the UNESCO Tokaj landscape.

sites.name: Makkoshotyka
sites.text: Makkoshotyka is a small upland village north-west of Sárospatak, at the forested edge of the Zemplén. It is one of the 27 Tokaj settlements, with few but cool vineyard slopes.

sites.name: Vámosújfalu
sites.text: Vámosújfalu ('customs new village') lies on the plain between Olaszliszka and Sárazsadány, its name recalling a medieval toll point. It is one of the quieter Tokaj settlements, with gentle slopes near the Bodrog.

sites.name: Tolcsva
sites.text: Tolcsva is one of Tokaj's great wine villages, with Oremus's winery and tunnel cellars, the headquarters of the state-owned Grand Tokaj (successor of the old state combine) and a wine museum. Sites such as Kincsem, Petrács and Kútpatka surround it, and noble rot was reportedly known here by 1527.

sites.name: Erdőhorváti
sites.text: Erdőhorváti is a forest village high in the Zemplén hills north of Tolcsva. Its few vineyards are among the coolest in the region, and the village is better known for its woods and walking routes than for wine.

sites.name: Bodrogolaszi
sites.text: Bodrogolaszi, another village named for its medieval Latin settlers, lies just south of Sárospatak. The Pajzos vineyard, one of the two historic estates of the Pajzos-Megyer winery, lies within its boundary.

sites.name: Golop
sites.text: Golop is a small village at the western margin of the region, between Tállya and Monok, on the edge of the Hernád valley. Its vineyards sit on the outer slopes of the Zemplén volcanic range.

sites.name: Monok
sites.text: Monok, at the far western rim of the Tokaj PDO, is famous as the birthplace of Lajos Kossuth (1802), leader of the 1848 revolution. Its vineyards face south over the Szerencs plain.

sites.name: Legyesbénye
sites.text: Legyesbénye is at the south-western end of the Tokaj crescent, near the Szerencs plain. It is a quiet village with gentle slopes, included among the 27 settlements of the PDO.

sites.name: Bekecs
sites.text: Bekecs, west of Szerencs, is one of the south-western edge villages of the region. Its gentle slopes give softer wines than the steep hills of Mád or Tarcal.

sites.name: Abaújszántó
sites.text: Abaújszántó marks the western end of Tokaj where the hills drop into the Hernád valley. Its Sátor-hegy ('Tent hill') and other volcanic slopes are farmed by the biodynamic Pendits estate, one of the region's early organic pioneers.

sites.name: Szerencs
sites.text: Szerencs is the gateway town at the south-western corner of Tokaj. The Rákóczi castle here hosted the 1605 diet that elected István Bocskai prince, and the town now includes Ond, whose Kőporos slope is a respected site. The town is also known for its chocolate factory.

sites.name: Sárazsadány
sites.text: Sárazsadány is a small village near the Bodrog between Vámosújfalu and Bodrogolaszi. It is one of the 27 Tokaj settlements, with gentle, botrytis-prone vineyards close to the river.

sites.name: Mézes Mály
sites.text: 'Honey pot' in old Hungarian, Mézes Mály in Tarcal was ranked a great first growth in the old classifications. About 19 ha of volcanic bedrock under deep loess on a warm south slope; Royal Tokaji owns about 11 ha and bottles both an Aszú and a dry Furmint from it. Its wines are rich and honeyed with a soft, broad texture from the loess.

sites.name: Szarvas
sites.text: Szarvas ('stag') lies on the southern foot of Tokaj hill between Tarcal and Tokaj and was rated a great first growth of the old classification. It was a royal and later Habsburg estate, and today belongs to the state-owned Grand Tokaj. Its loess and andesite give powerful, early-ripening aszú.

sites.name: Szent Tamás
sites.text: Named after St Thomas, this first-class Mád hillside of red nyirok clay and rhyolite tuff makes tense, smoky, saline wines. Szepsy's and the Szent Tamás winery's dry Furmints and Royal Tokaji's Aszú are its best-known bottlings.

sites.name: Úrágya
sites.text: Úrágya ('the lord's bed') lies on a high, steep slope north of Mád, on quartz-rich, silicified volcanic rock. Szepsy's and Királyudvar's dry Úrágya Furmint 2000 helped launch the dry single-vineyard movement, and the site still makes some of the most austere, long-lived dry wines in Tokaj.

sites.name: Betsek
sites.text: Betsek (also spelled Becsek) is a large first-class site east of Mád toward Bodrogkeresztúr, on rhyolite tuff and clay. Royal Tokaji's 1990 Betsek Aszú was among its first releases, and Dobogó and Szepsy also make wines from it.

sites.name: Király
sites.text: Király ('king') rises above Mád on rhyolite and red clay. Its steep upper part, Öreg Király ('old king'), was cleared and re-terraced by the Barta family from 2003 and is one of the steepest vineyards in the region; Szepsy also has parcels.

sites.name: Nyulászó
sites.text: Nyulászó ('hare-hunting place') is a first-class Mád site of volcanic clay that Royal Tokaji blends into its Aszú and bottles separately in good years. Its wines tend to be fine and spicy.

sites.name: Birsalmás
sites.text: Birsalmás ('quince orchard') lies on the western side of Mád. Royal Tokaji counts it among its first growths, and its name matches the quince note that classic Furmint often carries.

sites.name: Percze
sites.text: Percze is a small site close to the village of Mád, on rhyolite tuff; the Szepsy family consider it one of their best plots and named their Mád restaurant after it.

sites.name: Danczka
sites.text: Danczka (Dancka in the official list) sits around the Danczka-tető hilltop west of Mád. Its stony, windy slopes make tight, mineral dry wines, bottled by several of the Mád Circle growers.

sites.name: Bomboly
sites.text: Bomboly is a cool, elevated site north-east of Mád, with volcanic tuff soils. Its name appears on several modern single-vineyard dry Furmints. Being higher and more exposed, it ripens later than the village slopes and keeps notably bright acidity.

sites.name: Veresek
sites.text: Veresek ('the red ones') takes its name from the reddish volcanic clay of this Mád slope near the Bodrogkeresztúr border. It is a source of concentrated aszú berries.

sites.name: Hold-völgy
sites.text: Hold-völgy ('moon valley') is a sheltered valley site at Mád, and gave its name to the Holdvölgy winery, which works it along with neighbouring first-class sites.

sites.name: Juharos
sites.text: Juharos ('maple wood') is a Mád site in the official dűlő list, on volcanic tuff north of the village, producing fresh, mineral Furmint. Its northern position gives slow ripening, which suits dry styles more than aszú in most years.

sites.name: Kővágó
sites.text: Kővágó ('stone-cutter') is a stony Mád dűlő east of the village whose name recalls old quarrying; it makes firm, concentrated Furmint. Cut stone from the hill once went into Mád's houses and cellars, and the soil is correspondingly thin and rocky.

sites.name: Lapis
sites.text: Lapis (Latin for 'stone') is a terraced rhyolite slope above Bodrogkeresztúr. Királyudvar's Lapis Furmint and 6 Puttonyos Aszú made it famous, and the site produces taut, stony wines.

sites.name: Sajgó
sites.text: Sajgó lies on the Bodrogkeresztúr side of the Mád border, on volcanic tuff and clay, and gives powerful aszú berries. The site sits on the gentle saddle where the Mád valley opens toward the Bodrog, so river mist reaches it easily.

sites.name: Bendecz
sites.text: Bendecz is a Bodrogkeresztúr site south of the village center, on mixed volcanic soils, used for both dry and sweet wines by local growers. Like much of Bodrogkeresztúr, it benefits from the morning fogs rising off the river directly below.

sites.name: Kapi
sites.text: Kapi is a historic site on the Mezőzombor side of the Mád road, included in Disznókő's estate. In top botrytis years Disznókő bottles a single-vineyard Kapi 6 Puttonyos Aszú.

sites.name: Disznókő
sites.text: The Disznókő ('boar's rock') vineyard, first recorded in 1413, takes its name from a large boulder on the slope. It was ranked a first growth in the 18th-century classifications and today forms a single 150 ha block owned by AXA Millésimes.

sites.name: Kassai
sites.text: Kassai (named after Košice) is a Tarcal site on Kassai-hegy, part loess and part volcanic. Kikelet's Stéphanie Berecz made it known for silky, aromatic dry Furmint and Hárslevelű from loess.

sites.name: Lónyai
sites.text: Lónyai, named after a noble family, is a loess-covered Tarcal slope whose dry Hárslevelű and Furmint from Kikelet are textbook loess wines: floral, round and fine.

sites.name: Váti
sites.text: Váti is a Tarcal site on the warm, loess-covered southern face of Tokaj hill, worked by Kikelet and others. The loess here is deep and fine, so the wines are perfumed, supple and approachable early, the opposite of Mád's flinty style.

sites.name: Mandulás
sites.text: Mandulás ('almond grove') is a Tarcal loess site on the warm southern side of Tokaj hill. Almond trees once grew between the vines, a sign of how sheltered and warm the slope is. The wines are soft and aromatic, typical of Tokaj hill's loess side.

sites.name: Előhegy
sites.text: Előhegy ('front hill') is a Tarcal hillside facing toward the Bodrog, on volcanic rock with loess patches. Its position on the hill's eastern flank catches the first morning sun and the Bodrog mists alike, a good combination for botrytis.

sites.name: Szentkereszt
sites.text: Szentkereszt ('holy cross') lies high on Tokaj hill above Tarcal, a mix of andesite and loess with long views over the Great Plain. It is one of the higher sites on Tokaj hill, so the wines combine loess softness with more lift and acidity.

sites.name: Hétszőlő
sites.text: Hétszőlő ('seven vineyards') was assembled from seven parcels by the Garai family in 1502 and later owned by Gáspár Károli, Gábor Bethlen, the Rákóczis and the Habsburgs. Its 55 ha of south-facing slopes on volcanic rock under loess now belong to Michel Reybier's Tokaj-Hétszőlő estate.

sites.name: Nagy-szőlő
sites.text: Nagy-szőlő ('big vineyard') is a loess site on the southern foot of Tokaj hill next to Hétszőlő. Its sheltered, low position by the Tisza floodplain makes it an early-ripening site with frequent botrytis.

sites.name: Teleki
sites.text: Teleki is a site on the southern foot of Tokaj hill near Hétszőlő, on loess-covered volcanic rock. It takes its name from the Teleki noble family, who held land in Tokaj, and shares the warm, loess-covered profile of its neighbour Hétszőlő.

sites.name: Padi-hegy
sites.text: Padi-hegy at Rátka is an andesite hill west of Mád whose slopes make structured, smoky Furmint. The hill's peak, Nagy-Padi, rises above the village, and its vineyards face south-east over the Mád valley.

sites.name: Hasznos
sites.text: Hasznos ('useful') is a Tállya site on andesite and volcanic tuff, known for firm, spicy wines. It lies on the hills north of the village toward Golop, a historically important part of the Rákóczi family's Tállya holdings.

sites.name: Kőporos (Ond)
sites.text: Kőporos ('stone dust') at Ond, now part of Szerencs, is a stony volcanic hillside whose name describes the powdery weathered rock underfoot. Ond's slopes face south over the Szerencs plain and were valued in the old classifications.

sites.name: Csirke-mál
sites.text: Csirke-mál ('chicken slope') in Bodrogkisfalud is a warm, sheltered south-facing site; 'mál' is an old word for a sunny hillside. Its warmth makes it a dependable source of ripe, botrytised fruit.

sites.name: Poklos
sites.text: Poklos is a Szegi site above the Bodrog, whose name hints at its hot ('hellish') sun exposure. The steep slope faces south over the river, so it gets both heat and the moisture that brings noble rot.

sites.name: Lőcse
sites.text: Lőcse, named after the Upper Hungarian town of Levoča, is a high Erdőbénye site of rhyolite tuff and loess where Béres makes fresh, mineral dry wines.

sites.name: Omlás
sites.text: Omlás ('landslide') is a steep Erdőbénye slope of weathered volcanic rock in the cool northern part of the region. Béres works it for dry Furmint with bright acidity, a reminder that the forested north of the region is markedly cooler than the south.

sites.name: Határi
sites.text: Határi ('border') sits on the line between Erdőbénye and Olaszliszka. Attila Homonna's dry Furmints from about 2005 drew attention to this forgotten, cool, stony slope.

sites.name: Csontos
sites.text: Csontos ('bony') is an Olaszliszka site whose name describes its stony, skeletal volcanic soil. Wines from such thin, rocky ground are typically tight and mineral, best after some years in bottle.

sites.name: Kincsem
sites.text: Kincsem ('my treasure') is a Tolcsva vineyard best known through Grand Tokaj and other Tolcsva producers; the name is shared with Hungary's legendary unbeaten racehorse.

sites.name: Petrács
sites.text: Petrács is a historic Tolcsva site belonging largely to Oremus, on volcanic soils above the village. The slope rises steeply behind Tolcsva and has long been prized for aszú berries.

sites.name: Kútpatka
sites.text: Kútpatka ('well's horseshoe') is a Tolcsva site whose fruit goes into Oremus's wines. It is a horseshoe-shaped hollow named for a well, and its sheltered bowl concentrates warmth.

sites.name: Pajzos
sites.text: The Pajzos vineyard lies in Bodrogolaszi just south of Sárospatak. Rated first class in 1772, its 107-ha estate was bought in 1991 by Jean-Louis Laborde's French group and is now the core of Pajzos-Megyer; its 1993 Esszencia earned a perfect score from the Wine Advocate.

sites.name: Megyer
sites.text: Megyer is a historic 110-ha vineyard on the hill above Végardó at Sárospatak. The French insurer GAN won it in the 1992 privatisation, and it was later merged with Pajzos. Its cooler northern position gives fresher, more aromatic wines.

sites.name: Oremus
sites.text: Oremus ('let us pray') is the vineyard on the castle hill of Sátoraljaújhely, owned by the Rákóczis. Legend makes it the source of Szepsi Laczkó Máté's first aszú (1631), and it was rated primae classis in 1772. Vega Sicilia's Tolcsva estate took its name.

sites.name: Royal Tokaji
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Hugh Johnson, Danish winemaker Peter Vinding-Diers and about 60 Mád growers, Royal Tokaji was the first Western joint venture of the post-Communist era. It bought grapes until 1993 and now farms about 100 to 112 ha, including Mézes Mály, Szent Tamás, Betsek, Nyulászó and Birsalmás, which it labels with their historic first-growth ranks.

sites.name: Disznókő
sites.text: AXA Millésimes bought Disznókő ('boar's rock', first recorded 1413) in 1992 and rebuilt the winery beside the old press house. The estate is a single 150 ha block on a south-facing volcanic slope, planted with Furmint, Hárslevelű, Zéta and Sárgamuskotály. Its Aszú, Kapi single vineyard and '1413' sweet wine are benchmarks.

sites.name: Oremus (Tolcsva winery)
sites.text: The Álvarez family of Vega Sicilia founded Tokaj Oremus in 1993 at Tolcsva. The wines age in old tunnel cellars cut into the rock under the winery. Its dry Mandolás Furmint (since 2000) helped launch the dry wine revival, while its Aszú and Eszencia are among the most polished in the region.

sites.name: Pajzos-Megyer (Sárospatak)
sites.class: Winery, Sárospatak (formerly Château Pajzos and Château Megyer)
sites.text: The French investment group CFGVT, led by Jean-Louis Laborde, began buying in Tokaj in 1991; GAN won the Megyer vineyard in 1992. Laborde merged both into Pajzos Zrt around 2000. The Pajzos Esszencias of 1993 and 1999 both received 100 points from the Wine Advocate. The winery is on Nagy Lajos utca in Sárospatak.

sites.name: Szepsy
sites.text: István Szepsy, from a family of growers that traces its Tokaj roots to the 1500s, released his first Aszú in 1991 and, from the 2000 vintage, the dry single-vineyard Furmints (Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Király and others) that redefined Tokaj. The family farms about 52 ha around Mád; his 6 Puttonyos 1999 is a Decanter 'wine legend'.

sites.name: Királyudvar
sites.text: Királyudvar ('royal court') occupies a historic royal court building in Tarcal. Anthony Hwang, owner of Domaine Huet in Vouvray, bought it in 1997; Zoltán Demeter and István Szepsy shaped its early wines. It farms biodynamically, and its Lapis vineyard Aszú and Cuvée Ilona late harvest are classics.

sites.name: Dobogó
sites.text: Dobogó is a small winery in the old town of Tokaj founded by Izabella Zwack, of the Unicum liqueur family, in the mid-1990s. It makes dry Furmint from Betsek, Aszú and the late-harvest Mylitta from first-class sites.

sites.name: Patricius
sites.text: Patricius was founded in 2000 by the Kékessy family in a restored 18th-century manor at Bodrogkisfalud. It owns about 85 ha in first-class sites and is known for dry Furmint, Katinka late harvest and long-aged Aszú.

sites.name: Grand Tokaj
sites.text: Grand Tokaj is the state-owned successor of the Communist-era Tokaj combine and the later Tokaj Kereskedőház, based at Tolcsva. It buys grapes from thousands of small growers and remains the region's largest producer, exporting to more than 30 countries. Its holdings include the great first growth Szarvas.

sites.name: Barta
sites.text: Károly Barta's family winery in Mád restored the abandoned, terraced Öreg Király ('old king') vineyard from 2003, one of the steepest slopes in Tokaj. The winery occupies an old Rákóczi-era mansion in the village.

sites.name: Samuel Tinon
sites.text: Samuel Tinon, from a Sainte-Croix-du-Mont winemaking family near Bordeaux, came to Tokaj in 1991 and settled at Olaszliszka. He is best known for reviving dry Szamorodni aged for years under a veil of yeast (flor), as well as long-macerated Aszú.

sites.name: Tokaj-Hétszőlő
sites.text: Tokaj-Hétszőlő owns 55 ha of the historic Hétszőlő vineyard on Tokaj hill. The French group GMF bought it in 1991; Michel Reybier, owner of Cos d'Estournel, has owned it since 2009. It is farmed organically and runs the Rákóczi cellar in Tokaj town for tastings.

sites.name: Holdvölgy
sites.text: Holdvölgy is a Mád estate founded in the 2000s with vineyards in Hold-völgy and neighbouring first-class sites. Its labyrinthine cellar under the village is used for tastings and ageing.

sites.name: Kikelet
sites.text: Kikelet ('springtime') is the small Tarcal estate of Stéphanie Berecz, who came from Bordeaux to work at Disznókő, and her husband Zsolt. Their dry Furmint and Hárslevelű from the loess sites Lónyai, Váti and Kassai showed how fine loess wines can be.

sites.name: Béres
sites.text: Béres farms about 45 ha in the cool northern sites around Erdőbénye, including Lőcse, Diókút and Omlás. Its winery sits among the vines above the village.

sites.name: Rákóczi Cellar, Sárospatak
sites.text: Beneath the Rákóczi castle in Sárospatak runs a cellar labyrinth of several branches cut into volcanic tuff, used by the princes to store the wine of their Hegyalja estates. Their Tokaji served as a diplomatic gift, notably to Louis XIV. The castle and cellar are now a museum and tasting venue.

sites.name: Rákóczi Castle, Sárospatak
sites.text: The Renaissance castle on the Bodrog was the seat of the Rákóczi princes, owners of great Tokaj vineyards. Zsuzsanna Lorántffy lived here, and Ferenc II Rákóczi led the 1703 to 1711 war of independence from these lands, using Tokaji as diplomatic currency.

sites.name: Rákóczi Cellar, Tokaj
sites.text: This cellar under Tokaj's main square, beside the church, dates from the early 15th century. Its knights' hall (28 m long, 10 m wide, 5 m high) is said to be the largest underground hall in the region. Its walls are coated with black cellar mould, and it is used today for tastings.

sites.name: Tokaj Museum
sites.text: The Tokaj Museum occupies an 18th-century Greek merchant's house in Tokaj town. Greek traders were key middlemen in the 18th-century Tokaji trade. Its exhibits cover the history of Tokaji wine, coopering and the town's Greek, Jewish and Hungarian communities.

sites.name: Kőporos cellar row, Hercegkút
sites.text: Two streets of cellars dug into the hill above Hercegkút (Kőporos and Gombos-hegy), most with small stone or plastered fronts, form part of the core zone of the UNESCO Tokaj landscape. They show the small-grower cellar culture of the German-speaking settlers.

sites.name: Szepsi Laczkó Máté Memorial House
sites.text: In Erdőbénye a small memorial house honours Máté Szepsi Laczkó (c. 1576 to 1632/33), the Reformed pastor credited by legend with the first aszú. Historians doubt the claim, since his own chronicle never mentions aszú, but the story remains central to Tokaj's identity.

sites.name: Mád Synagogue
sites.text: This late-18th-century baroque synagogue in Mád, restored in the 2000s, recalls the Jewish families who dominated the Tokaji trade, produced kosher wine for Polish and Russian markets and owned many cellars until the Holocaust.

sites.name: Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape (UNESCO)
sites.text: UNESCO inscribed the Tokaj landscape in 2002, with a core area of 13,255 ha and a buffer of 74,879 ha. It recognises a living tradition of viticulture and winemaking, with its pattern of vineyards, villages and rock-cut cellars. The point marks the summit of Tokaj hill (Kopasz-hegy, 514 m).

sites.name: Eger Castle
sites.text: In 1552 István Dobó's garrison of about 2,000 held Eger castle for 39 days against a far larger Ottoman army. Later legend says red wine stained the defenders' beards and the Turks thought they drank bull's blood, the story behind Egri Bikavér. Eger fell in 1596 and stayed Ottoman until 1687.

sites.name: Szépasszony-völgy
sites.text: The 'Valley of the Beautiful Woman' on the south-west edge of Eger is lined with around 200 cellars cut into soft rhyolite tuff, many now tasting rooms. It is the classic place to taste Egri Bikavér from the barrel, and the name's origin (a pagan goddess, a beautiful innkeeper) is still argued over.

sites.name: Nagy-Eged
sites.text: Nagy-Eged is the steep limestone and tuff hill north-east of Eger, rising to about 535 m, with south-facing terraces. It is considered the town's finest red-wine site, especially for Kékfrankos and Pinot Noir, and features in many Grand Superior Bikavérs.

sites.name: Villány cellar row and Wine Museum
sites.text: Villány's Baross Gábor and Batthyány streets are lined with the cellars and press houses of the German-descended families who rebuilt the area after the Ottoman wars. The Wine Museum occupies an 18th-century cellar in the middle of the row.

sites.name: Palkonya cellar village
sites.text: Palkonya's whitewashed press houses, about 50 of them, run in a row along a single lane below the vines. The village, settled by Swabians, is one of the best-preserved small cellar villages in the Villány district.

sites.name: Kopár
sites.text: Kopár ('bare') is a steep, stony south-facing limestone slope at Nagyharsány. Its name describes how thin the topsoil is. Gere Attila's flagship red, a Cabernet Franc-led blend, is named after it, and it remains Villány's best-known single vineyard.

sites.name: Jammertal
sites.text: Jammertal ('valley of lamentation') is a historic Villány vineyard. Its name is said to recall a battle near here in the 1687 campaign. It is now planted with Cabernet Franc and other reds and is home to the Jammertal hotel and winery.

sites.name: Heimann & Fiai
sites.text: The Heimann family estate in the Iván valley near Szekszárd has led the revival of Kadarka, collecting and replanting old local clones. It also makes some of the district's finest Bikavér and Cabernet Franc.

sites.name: Somló hill
sites.text: A lone extinct volcano rising to 432 m out of the flat Kisalföld, Somló is topped by a castle ruin and wrapped in small vineyards and press houses. Its basalt soils give Hungary's most mineral whites, the Juhfark-led 'wedding night wine' said to guarantee a son.

sites.name: Badacsony hill
sites.text: Badacsony is a coffin-shaped basalt butte on the north shore of Lake Balaton. Its columnar basalt 'organ pipes' tower over terraces of Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát and Kéknyelű, and poet Sándor Kisfaludy's press house still stands on its slope.

sites.name: Szent György-hegy
sites.text: Szent György-hegy (415 m) near Tapolca is a basalt witness hill whose columnar 'organ pipes' and old press houses make it one of the most beautiful vineyard hills in Hungary. Its wines are part of the Badacsony PDO.

sites.name: Tihany Benedictine Abbey
sites.text: Founded in 1055 by King Andrew I, the abbey on the Tihany peninsula owned vineyards from its first charter. That charter is famous for containing the oldest surviving written Hungarian words. The peninsula is now a red-wine PDO.

sites.name: Pannonhalma Archabbey Winery
sites.text: The Benedictine archabbey founded in 996, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996, has grown wine for a millennium. Its modern winery, rebuilt in 2003 on the old vineyard terraces, makes Rajnai rizling, Sauvignon Blanc, Tramini and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Törley, Budafok
sites.text: József Törley learned sparkling winemaking in Reims and in 1882 moved his business to Budafok on the southern edge of Budapest, attracted by its limestone cellars and nearby vineyards. Törley remains Hungary's biggest sparkling wine house; the family's mansion is nearby.

sites.name: Hajós cellar village
sites.text: Outside the village of Hajós lies a separate 'village' of more than 1,200 cellars and press houses in neat streets, built by Swabian settlers from the 18th century. It is one of the largest cellar villages in Central Europe and hosts a festival every May.

sites.name: Fertőrákos quarry
sites.text: This Leitha limestone quarry beside Lake Fertő has been worked since Roman times. Stone from here helped build Vienna, and its huge cavern halls are part of the Fertő/Neusiedlersee UNESCO landscape. The same limestone underlies some of Sopron's Kékfrankos vineyards.

sites.name: Kecskemét and the sand vineyards
sites.text: Kecskemét is the hub of the Kunság. In 1883 the town gave the state land for the Miklóstelep demonstration vineyard, which proved that vines on loose sand escape phylloxera. Commissioner Gyula Miklós's experiment made the Great Plain Hungary's largest vineyard.

sites.name: Aldebrő and Feldebrő
sites.text: The twin villages of Aldebrő and Feldebrő at the eastern foot of the Mátra are the heart of the Debrői Hárslevelű PDO. Feldebrő's church has a crypt with 11th-century frescoes, among the oldest in Hungary.

sites.name: Csopak
sites.text: Csopak lies on the north-east shore of Lake Balaton among slopes of red Permian sandstone and slate. Its growers' 2012 'Csopak Codex' and the 2020 Csopak PDO made Olaszrizling a serious terroir wine.

sites.name: Kőszeg
sites.text: Kőszeg is a walled town on the Austrian border with its own PDO since 2025. Every year since 1740 the town has drawn the length of the young vine shoots on St George's Day into its 'Book of the Coming of the Grapes', a rare record of budbreak.

sites.name: Stara trta (Old Vine), Maribor
sites.text: Trained along the south facade of a house in Maribor's Lent quarter, this Žametovka vine is more than 400 years old and listed by Guinness as the oldest vine in the world. It still gives 35 to 55 kg of grapes a year, enough for 15 to 35 litres of wine. Cuttings grow at 130 official sites in Slovenia and 84 abroad.

sites.name: Ptujska klet, Ptuj
sites.text: Ptuj's winery claims a symbolic beginning in 1239, when the Minorites built a monastery with a wine cellar in the town centre. Its archive holds Zlata trta 1917, the oldest Slovenian archive wine, hidden from the occupiers in World War II by Pavel Ornig.

sites.name: Vinag cellar, Maribor
sites.text: Under Maribor's Trg svobode lies a vast cellar network on several levels, among the largest in Central Europe. It was the core of Vinag, the city's big socialist-era wine company, and is now used for tours, tastings and ageing.

sites.name: Jeruzalem
sites.text: A hilltop hamlet in the Ljutomer-Ormož hills, Jeruzalem is said to have been named by crusaders who saw it as a promised land. Its steep, terraced amphitheatres of Šipon, Laški rizling, Sauvignon and Traminec are among the most photographed vineyards in Slovenia.

sites.name: Haloze hills
sites.text: The Haloze hills south of Ptuj, along the Croatian border, are among the steepest vineyard landscapes in Central Europe. Small terraced plots on marl give racy Laški rizling, Šipon and Sauvignon.

sites.name: Radgonske gorice, Gornja Radgona
sites.text: Gornja Radgona's winery traces its sparkling-wine tradition to 1852, when Clotar Bouvier began making traditional-method wine here. Its Zlata Radgonska penina is Slovenia's best-known sparkling brand, aged in cellars cut into the hill.

sites.name: Lendavske gorice
sites.text: The vineyard hill above Lendava in Prekmurje looks out over the Pannonian plain to Hungary and Croatia, with a wooden lookout tower and traditional press houses among Laški rizling and Šipon vines.

sites.name: Movia
sites.text: The Kristančič family's estate in Ceglo has made wine since 1820, with vineyards on both sides of the Italian border. Aleš Kristančič made it famous for long-macerated Lunar Rebula and Puro, a sparkling wine sold undisgorged.

sites.name: Klinec
sites.text: Aleks Klinec's estate and guesthouse in Medana farms biodynamically and makes long-macerated whites (Rebula, Malvazija, Jakot) aged in acacia, mulberry and cherry wood, a reference for Brda orange wine.

sites.name: Kabaj
sites.text: Frenchman Jean-Michel Morel married into the Kabaj family at Šlovrenc in Brda; their macerated Rebula and Amfora wines, fermented in Georgian qvevri, helped build Slovenian orange wine's international profile.

sites.name: Edi Simčič
sites.text: This Vipolže estate on the Italian border is one of Brda's leading names. Its single-vineyard Kozana Chardonnay and Duet Lex Merlot-based reds show the district's capacity for structured, ageable wines.

sites.name: Dobrovo Castle and Klet Brda
sites.text: Dobrovo's Renaissance castle anchors Goriška Brda's capital village. Klet Brda, the cooperative founded here in 1957, gathers around 400 growers and is Slovenia's largest wine producer.

sites.name: Batič
sites.text: The Batič family's biodynamic estate at Šempas in the Vipava valley makes macerated whites, the Zaria blend and Angel, a sweet white. It was among the Vipava pioneers of skin contact and natural winemaking.

sites.name: Tomaj and Dutovlje, the Teran villages
sites.text: Tomaj and neighbouring Dutovlje sit at the heart of Teran country on the Kras, among red-earth vineyards walled in limestone. Family osmice (seasonal farm taverns) pour Teran with pršut.

sites.name: Bizeljsko repnice
sites.text: Bizeljsko's repnice are caves dug by hand into quartz sand beneath the vineyards, first for storing turnips and later wine and sparkling wine, which keep at a steady temperature. Several, such as Najger's, are open for tastings.

sites.name: Trška gora
sites.text: Trška gora, a hill above Novo mesto crowned by a pilgrimage church, is covered with small vineyards and zidanice cottages: the classic Cviček landscape of Dolenjska.

sites.name: Metlika
sites.text: Metlika on the Kolpa is the wine capital of Bela krajina and home of Metliška črnina. Its castle houses the Slovenian Fire-Fighting Museum and a regional museum with viticulture exhibits, and the town's wine fair each spring showcases the district.

sites.name: Dingač vineyards
sites.text: The south face of the Pelješac ridge above the sea between Trstenik and Borak: 45-degree slopes of dolomite scree planted with bush-trained Plavac Mali. Protected since 1961, it was Croatia's first appellation. The vines bake under direct sun, reflected light from the sea and heat from the stones.

sites.name: Dingač tunnel, Potomje
sites.text: The 400 m single-lane tunnel through the Pelješac ridge opened on 29 November 1975, financed by the Potomje growers' cooperative. It replaced the donkey path over the pass and cut the trip from village to vineyard from 20 km to about 4.

sites.name: Postup
sites.text: West of Dingač near Donja Banda, Postup is another steep south-facing slope of Plavac Mali above the sea. It was protected in 1967 and is often considered slightly fresher and more elegant than Dingač.

sites.name: Grgić Vina, Trstenik
sites.text: Miljenko 'Mike' Grgić, the Croatian-born winemaker of the Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay that won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, returned to his homeland in 1996 to found this winery at Trstenik on Pelješac, making Plavac Mali and Pošip.

sites.name: Kaštel Novi, Zinfandel's rediscovery
sites.text: In 2001 DNA from nine old vines of Crljenak Kaštelanski in a vineyard at Kaštel Novi, between Split and Trogir, matched California Zinfandel. The UC Davis team of Carole Meredith worked with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of Zagreb. The variety, also called Tribidrag, has since been replanted around Kaštela.

sites.name: Smokvica, Korčula
sites.text: Smokvica and neighbouring Čara in the middle of Korčula are the home of Pošip, a rich, golden white said to have been found as a chance seedling in the 19th century. Their karst fields hold most of the island's Pošip.

sites.name: Lumbarda, Korčula
sites.text: On the sandy eastern tip of Korčula, Lumbarda grows Grk, a white whose flowers are functionally female, so Plavac Mali is interplanted as a pollinator. The sand, rare on this limestone coast, gives a dry, bitter-edged, saline white.

sites.name: Stari Grad Plain, Hvar
sites.text: Greek colonists from Paros founded Pharos in 384 BC and divided the fertile plain into rectangular plots bounded by stone walls. Those plots are still farmed with vines and olives 2,400 years later, and the plain has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

sites.name: Vis island
sites.text: Vis, ancient Issa, was a Greek colony from the 4th century BC and later a closed military island until 1989. Its white Vugava and the red Plavac Mali grow in the island's interior fields.

sites.name: Bucavac, Primošten
sites.text: The vineyards above Primošten are a lacework of tiny plots carved out of bare limestone and walled with the stones removed to plant them. They are famous for Babić. A photograph of them is said to have hung in the UN headquarters as a monument to human labour.

sites.name: Ponikve plateau, Pelješac
sites.text: The karst plateau of Ponikve above Ston at the neck of Pelješac became Croatia's 17th wine PDO in 2021, for Plavac Mali, Pošip and Maraština, including wine from raisined grapes.

sites.name: Kutjevo castle and the 1232 cellar
sites.text: Cistercian monks built the Kutjevo cellar in 1232. The baroque manor beside it later belonged to the Jesuits and then the Turković family, who began the wine archive in the late 19th century. Kutjevo's archive now holds over 65,000 bottles, the oldest a 1947 Pinot Blanc.

sites.name: Ilok Old Cellar (Iločki podrumi)
sites.text: Beneath Ilok castle on the Danube, the Old Cellar dates to 1450. Its 1947 Traminac is said to have been served at Queen Elizabeth II's coronation in 1953. Looted during the 1991 to 1998 occupation, it was restored and is again the heart of Iločki podrumi.

sites.name: Erdut
sites.text: Erdutski vinogradi works several hundred hectares on the loess bluff of Erdut above the Danube, where a medieval tower watches over the vines. Its cellar holds one of the largest oak casks in Europe.

sites.name: Momjan
sites.text: A hilltop village above Buje in north-west Istria, Momjan gives its name to the Muškat momjanski PDO (2021). Kozlović's winery sits in the valley below, among some of Istria's best Malvazija sites.

sites.name: Motovun
sites.text: The walled hill town of Motovun overlooks the Mirna valley, with Malvazija and Teran vineyards on its slopes and truffle oak forests below. Roxanich and other estates are nearby.

sites.name: Plešivica wine road
sites.text: The Plešivica hills near Jastrebarsko are lined with family wineries making traditional-method sparkling, Riesling and amphora wines. Tomac first buried qvevri-style amphorae here in the 2000s.

sites.name: Sremski Karlovci
sites.text: This baroque town at the foot of Fruška Gora was the seat of the Serbian Orthodox metropolitans and the place where the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz was signed. It is the home of Bermet, a dessert wine flavoured with about 20 herbs and spices, made only by a few families.

sites.name: Živanović winery and Beekeeping Museum
sites.text: The Živanović family's 300-year-old cellar in Sremski Karlovci makes Bermet, said to have been stocked on the Titanic in 1912. The family also runs Serbia's only private beekeeping museum, honouring Jovan Živanović, a pioneer of modern beekeeping.

sites.name: King's Winery, Oplenac
sites.text: King Alexander I built this winery at the foot of Oplenac hill in Topola in 1931. It has two underground floors kept at 8 °C and 99 oak casks. A barrel of over 4,000 litres from King Peter I's first winery of 1909 survives. Replanted vineyards gave their first harvest in 2006.

sites.name: Rajac pivnice
sites.text: The cellar settlement of Rajac stands about 2 km west of the village on Beli Breg hill. Stone cellars with arched portals line winding lanes beside a cemetery of about 200 19th-century tombstones. It is part of the Negotin Pivnice on Serbia's UNESCO Tentative List.

sites.name: Rogljevo pivnice
sites.text: On a hill north of Rajac, Rogljevo's cellar village has about 122 structures along two parallel roads. About 40 are still used for wine and some as taverns. Forty cellars were built between 1859 and 1890.

sites.name: Vršački vinogradi
sites.text: The Vršac wine company's headquarters on Svetosavski trg and its 1968 'New Cellar', with a capacity of 2,000 wagons (about 20 million litres), once among the largest in Europe, anchor the Banat's wine history.

sites.name: Aleksandrovac
sites.text: Aleksandrovac in the Župa valley calls itself Serbia's wine capital. It has held the Župska berba harvest festival each September since 1963 and has a museum of viticulture and winemaking. Prokupac and Tamjanika are its grapes.

sites.name: Gudurica
sites.text: Gudurica, about 25 km east of Vršac, was a German-speaking village (Kudritz) and is now the centre of the Vršac hills' boutique wineries. Its slopes on the eastern edge of the Vršac hills catch more rain and cooler air than the town's vineyards.

sites.name: Tvrdoš Monastery winery
sites.text: The Serbian Orthodox monastery of Tvrdoš on the Trebišnjica near Trebinje dates from the late 15th or early 16th century. One of its wine cellars is from the 15th century, and the monks still make Vranac and a flinty Žilavka, with a monk as cellar master.

sites.name: Vukoje, Trebinje
sites.text: Radovan Vukoje harvested his first grapes in 2000 and built one of Herzegovina's largest private wineries near Trebinje, on land that was once part of Emperor Franz Joseph's personal vineyard. Its pure Vranac and Žilavka are benchmarks.

sites.name: Podrumi Andrija, Paoča (Čitluk)
sites.text: The Ćorić family's winery at Paoča near Čitluk made Žilavka for Tito under special permission in the socialist era and kept working through the 1990s war. Its Blatina Andrija Selection is a reference for the grape.

sites.name: Vinarija Čitluk
sites.text: Čitluk is Herzegovina's largest wine municipality, and Vinarija Čitluk its biggest producer. Its Žilavka and Blatina come from the stony Brotnjo plateau, which includes the pilgrimage village of Međugorje.

sites.name: Mostar
sites.text: Mostar, with its rebuilt Old Bridge (UNESCO), is the regional capital and starting point of the Herzegovina Wine Route. The Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina names come from the vineyards around it.

sites.name: Ćemovsko polje vineyard (Plantaže)
sites.text: South-east of Podgorica, Plantaže's single vineyard on the stony Ćemovsko polje covers more than 2,300 ha with some 11 million vines. It is one of the largest single vineyard blocks in Europe, planted mainly with Vranac, Kratošija, Krstač and international grapes.

sites.name: Šipčanik cellar
sites.text: Under Plantaže's Ćemovsko polje vineyard lies Šipčanik, a 356 m winding tunnel more than 30 m underground. It was built as a military facility of the former airfield. Since November 2007 it has held oak casks instead of aircraft: over 2 million litres of wine at 17 to 19 °C, plus an archive of 18,000 bottles.

sites.name: Virpazar and Crmnica
sites.text: Virpazar, on the shore of Lake Skadar, is the centre of Crmnica, whose terraced vineyards made Montenegro's most prized wine in the 19th century. Family cellars in Godinje and Limljani still make Vranac and Kratošija.

sites.name: Budva
sites.text: The walled town of Budva on the Adriatic gave its name to the medieval statute (1426 to 1442) that first records 'Cratosia', probably today's Kratošija. Geneticists now consider this the likely origin of Zinfandel.

sites.name: Tikveš winery, Kavadarci
sites.text: Tikveš winery in Kavadarci dates its founding to 1885. It became a cooperative after 1946, was privatised with new owners in 2003, and calls itself the largest winery in South-Eastern Europe. Its Barovo and Bela Voda single-vineyard reds are named after Tikveš localities.

sites.name: Stobi archaeological site
sites.text: The ruins of Stobi, a Paeonian, Macedonian and Roman city at the confluence of the Crna and Vardar rivers, include mosaics with vines and drinking scenes. They are a reminder that the Vardar valley has made wine for well over two thousand years.

sites.name: Stobi winery
sites.text: Founded in the 2000s near Gradsko and named after the nearby Roman city, Stobi is one of the most modern wineries in the Vardar valley. It makes Vranec, Žilavka, Temjanika and Bordeaux varieties.

sites.name: Popova Kula, Demir Kapija
sites.text: Popova Kula, on a hill above Demir Kapija ('iron gate') where the Vardar cuts through a gorge, is a winery and guesthouse that has championed the local red Stanušina.

sites.name: Kallmet
sites.text: The village of Kallmet near Lezhë gave its name to Albania's most famous native red grape, grown on the surrounding Zadrima plain and hills. The village is part of the Catholic north, where vineyards survived the Ottoman centuries.

sites.name: Çobo winery
sites.text: The Çobo family winery at Ura Vajgurore near Berat is one of Albania's best-known estates, championing the local white Pulës and the red Shesh i Zi.

sites.name: Kokomani winery
sites.text: Kantina Kokomani at Ndroq, west of Tirana, is a modern family winery making Shesh and international varieties from the coastal hills between the capital and Durrës.

sites.name: Nurellari winery
sites.text: Nurellari's winery near Poliçan in the Osum valley of Skrapar, south-east of Berat, makes wines from local and international grapes in Albania's rugged southern interior.

sites.name: Stone Castle, Rahovec
sites.text: Founded in 1952 as Rahovec's large wine combine, the winery was privatised in 2006 for €5.5 million and renamed Stone Castle. With 10 to 13 million litres of capacity and the ability to process about 70,000 tonnes of grapes a season, it is one of the largest private wineries in Europe.

sites.name: Rahovec
sites.text: Rahovec (Orahovac) is Kosovo's wine capital. Its municipality holds about 2,465 of the country's 3,400 ha of vineyard on sunny hills at 300 to 600 m, with many small family cellars alongside Stone Castle.

sites.name: Cotnari winery
sites.text: Cotnari's main winery sits below the hill where Stephen the Great kept his court cellars. The company farms one of Romania's largest single vineyards of Grasă, Fetească Albă, Tămâioasă and Frâncușă and keeps a large archive of sweet wines, some decades old.

sites.name: Cotnari, Cătălina hill
sites.text: On Cătălina hill above Cotnari stood a Geto-Dacian fortress about 2,500 years ago; finds suggest viticulture dates to Burebista's time. The town later held one of Moldavia's largest fairs and a Latin school founded by Despot Vodă in 1562.

sites.name: Sarmizegetusa Regia
sites.text: The mountain capital of the Dacian kingdom in the Orăștie Mountains, a UNESCO site. According to Strabo, Burebista and his priest Decaeneus ordered the Dacians' vines destroyed, Europe's earliest recorded anti-wine edict.

sites.name: Tropaeum Traiani, Adamclisi
sites.text: This Roman victory monument was raised in 109 AD to celebrate Trajan's conquest of Dacia. It gives its name to Adamclisi, Romania's newest wine DOC (2020).

sites.name: Bethlen-Haller Castle, Cetatea de Baltă (Jidvei)
sites.text: This Renaissance castle on the Târnava Mică was built for the Bethlen family in the 17th century. It now serves as the headquarters and showpiece of Jidvei, Romania's largest single wine estate, with about 2,500 ha of Transylvanian vineyards.

sites.name: Cramele Recaș
sites.text: Rebuilt after 1998 by Romanian and British partners, Cramele Recaș is one of the largest and most modern wineries in Romania, with about 1,000 ha near Timișoara. Recaș's vineyards date from the 15th century.

sites.name: Prince Știrbey
sites.text: The Știrbey princely family's estate at Drăgășani was nationalised under Communism and restituted in 2001. Ileana Kripp-Costinescu and the Austrian winemaker Oliver Bauer revived it, championing Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Tămâioasă and Novac.

sites.name: LacertA
sites.text: LacertA, named for a protected lizard of the Dealu Mare hills, is a modern estate at Năeni whose Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux blends exemplify the new Dealu Mare.

sites.name: Valea Călugărească
sites.text: The 'Valley of the Monks' in Dealu Mare has long housed Romania's national viticulture research institute. Phylloxera was first recorded nearby at Chitorani in the 1880s, which makes this valley the starting point of modern Romanian vine growing.

sites.name: Pietroasele
sites.text: Pietroasele at the east end of Dealu Mare is famous for sweet Tămâioasă Românească and for the Pietroasa Treasure, a 4th-century Gothic gold hoard found here in 1837.

sites.name: Murfatlar winery
sites.text: Murfatlar's winery and research station near Constanța made the name famous under Communism for rich, late-harvest Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Muscat Ottonel from chalky, sun-baked hills.

sites.name: Domeniul Coroanei Segarcea
sites.text: Segarcea was the Romanian royal family's crown wine domain from 1884. It was nationalised in 1948 and revived as a private estate in the 2000s, making Cabernet Sauvignon and Tămâioasă roză.

sites.name: Panciu
sites.text: Panciu in northern Vrancea is Romania's sparkling-wine town, with cellars holding millions of bottles. It was rebuilt after a 1940 earthquake and lies near the World War I battlefield of Mărășești.

sites.name: Odobești
sites.text: Odobești is the centre of one of the oldest and largest vineyard areas in Romania, on the slopes of the Măgura Odobești in Vrancea, home of the tart local white Galbenă de Odobești.

sites.name: Banu Mărăcine station
sites.text: The University of Craiova's teaching and research vineyard on the city's outskirts gives its name to the small Banu Mărăcine DOC. It is named after a medieval Oltenian boyar, and its vines are used for student training and clonal trials.

sites.name: Crama Oprișor
sites.text: Crama Oprișor at Oprișor in Mehedinți, in Romania's far south-west near the Danube, was one of the first modern estates of the 2000s. It is known for structured Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux blends such as La Cetate, from warm, south-facing slopes.

sites.name: Kordopulov House, Melnik
sites.text: Built in 1754 for wine production and later owned by the Greek merchant Manolis Kordopoulos, this house in Melnik has a tunnel cellar cut into the sandstone with ventilation shafts and channels. It can hold about 300 tonnes of wine, and its largest cask holds 12.5 tonnes. It is now a museum and tasting room.

sites.name: Melnik Earth Pyramids
sites.text: Rain has carved Neogene sandstone capped with reddish conglomerate into towers, mushrooms and obelisks up to 100 m high around Melnik. They are a natural landmark since 1960, covering about 17 km². The town's wine cellars are dug into the same soft rock.

sites.name: Melnik
sites.text: Bulgaria's smallest town, with about 400 people, Melnik once had some 20,000 and traded wine to Venice, Austria and England. It lies among the earth pyramids at the foot of the Pirin, and Broadleaf Melnik is grown in the surrounding valleys.

sites.name: Rozhen Monastery
sites.text: About 6 km north-east of Melnik, Rozhen is the largest monastery in the Pirin region, with roots in the medieval period. Vines grow on the slopes below it, and a trellis of old vines shades its courtyard.

sites.name: Thracian temple of Chetinyova Mogila, Starosel
sites.text: This Thracian temple under a mound near Starosel dates from the late 5th to early 4th century BC. It is the largest of six underground temples in the Starosel complex, found in 2000. A local winery has built its identity around the Thracian cult of wine.

sites.name: Starosel wine complex
sites.text: A winery, hotel and spa outside Starosel, built in Thracian-revival style with cellars dug into the hillside. It makes reds and whites under the Hisarya PDO near the village's Thracian temples.

sites.name: Perperikon
sites.text: A rock-cut sacred city on a 470 m hill near Kardzhali in the Eastern Rhodopes, occupied from about 5000 BC to the 14th century. A famous temple of Dionysus is thought to have stood here, and its rock altar is almost 2 m across.

sites.name: Magura Cave and winery
sites.text: Magura Cave near Rabisha in the north-west has prehistoric paintings in bat guano. Since the 1980s it has also housed the cellar of a traditional-method sparkling wine, aged in the cave's constant 12 °C.

sites.name: Pleven Wine Museum, Kaylaka
sites.text: Pleven's wine museum occupies a natural cave in Kaylaka park, displaying several thousand bottles and the history of Bulgarian winemaking. Pleven's institute bred Rubin in 1944.

sites.name: Suhindol
sites.text: This hill village in the central north founded Bulgaria's first wine cooperative, 'Gamza', in 1909. In the 1980s its Cabernet Sauvignon was a bestseller on British supermarket shelves.

sites.name: Asenovgrad
sites.text: Asenovgrad, at the mouth of the Chaya gorge below the Rhodopes, is the traditional capital of Mavrud. The legend of Khan Krum and the brave youth Mavrud is set here. The medieval Asen fortress and Bachkovo Monastery are nearby.

sites.name: Sungurlare valley
sites.text: The Sungurlare valley in the eastern Balkan foothills is the home of Red Misket (Misket Cherven). This pink-skinned aromatic white gives delicate, floral wines, and the town holds a wine festival each autumn.

sites.name: Euxinograd Palace
sites.text: Euxinograd, the former royal summer palace on the coast north of Varna, was built in the 1880s for Prince Alexander of Battenberg. Its park and estate vineyards give their name to a small PDO.

sites.name: Brestovitsa
sites.text: A village south-west of Plovdiv on the Rhodope foothills, known for Rubin and Mavrud. Georgiev & Milkov make Rubin here, and the area once supplied the Plovdiv export cellars.
